bodyText:
Happiness filled me so completely that night, I never thought to question it.
I was lingering beneath the banquet hall's chandeliers, a champagne flute balanced between my fingers, while contentment warmed me from the inside out. Laughter rolled through the crowded room. Glasses chimed together, and passing guests left trails of costly perfume, sharp cologne, and effortless wealth.
This was the future I had chosen, and every part of me wanted it.
Most of all, I loved watching Julian thrive. His tailored suit sharpened the breadth of his shoulders, and confidence made him seem taller as he accepted praise from investors and business partners. He laughed without restraint, perfectly at ease among people eager for his attention.
Rooms like this suited him. He never needed to demand notice; it gathered around him naturally.
Soon, he would belong to me without qualification.
The delay was mine to own. Although we had been together for six years, I still had not revealed what I truly was. I had become the only mother his children remembered, yet he did not know that a wolf lived beneath my skin too.
Whenever I considered confessing, Kira urged patience. One more day, she would insist. One more landmark in our life together, and then we could tell him.
My husband was Julian Miller, the future Alpha of the Silver Moon pack. We had met in college, when I was a gifted chemistry student and he was a businessman searching for an intern at Brightwell Nutrition.
I have always known that claiming my fated mate could never be part of my life. Then Julian appeared: an intelligent, magnetic Alpha who wanted to marry me despite the unremarkable human identity I wore.
It had felt less like chance than a story written for my benefit.
He was raising twins alone. I never learned exactly what had happened to his fated mate, but I believed the moon goddess had offered me another path toward the family I could not stop wanting.
There had been no waiting, no slow construction. Julian and his children had given me a family all at once.
Our home was not flawless. Still, I loved him, and I loved the twins who now felt like my own, more fiercely than I loved anyone else.
The music dropped to a mur. When a spoon rang against crystal, anticipation fluttered through me instead of anxiety. I recognized what was about to happen and moved before Julian had the opportunity, raising my glass as I stepped into view.
"May I steal everyone's attention? Only for a minute."
Conversation dissolved. Faces turned toward me from every corner of the hall.
Surprise crossed Julian's expression before affection replaced it. His smile was warm and faintly indulgent, the one he often gave me when I assumed control of life's smaller moments.
"I won't make a long speech," I said. "There is simply someone here who deserves to know how proud I am of him."
The guests responded with quiet approval. I shifted toward Julian and held his gaze.
"This launch has not come easily. Anyone who has spent time near Julian during the past year has seen what it demanded from him: sleepless nights, endless pressure, and more than a few arguments with his own stubborness."
Julian shook his head while laughter moved through the room.
"But tonight makes one thing clear," I went on. "Vision means something when a person has the determination to defend it. Integrity means something too. And Brightwell Nutrition, the company Julian built, is ready to improve people's lives."
The applause came hard and sincere.
I extended my flute toward him. "For Julian, for Brightwell Nutrition, and for everything still ahead of us."
"Everything ahead," the crowd answered.
Julian bent close enough to brush a familiar kiss across my cheek.
"Thank you," he whispered. "Somehow, you always find the right words."
I trusted that he meant it.
More importantly, I trusted what were together.
His new supplement was already exceeding expectations. Favorable reports were arriving sooner than anyone had predicted, documenting stronger fertility indicators and pregnancies in their earliest stages. The investors could barely contain their excitement, while physicians remained guarded but interested.
Nobody asked who had first conceived the formula.
I did not mind.
Brightwell Nutrition belonged to Julian, so its triumph could belong to him as well. Aplause was never what I needed. My compensation waited at home in the life we shared: the familiar rooms, the dependable rituals, and two children tucked safely into their beds each night.
Across the hall, Emily and Oscar occupied a low table scattered with crayons and coloring books. A pack nanny remained close while they drew. Emily noticed me looking and waved with her entire arm; beside her, Oscar displayed the new gap in his grin.
Love tightened painfully beneath my ribs.
For once, everything seemed stable. I felt protected, as though each difficult compromise I had made had finally proved worthwhile.
At first, the woman's arrival escaped my notice.
One of Julian's partners had cornered me with a discussion about market forecasts, and I was offering polite nods while he spoke. Then the room's rhythm altered. Nothing stopped outright, but laughter faltered and conversations sank into cautious murmurs.
Unease pulled something taut inside me.
I followed the attention toward the doors.
A woman had paused just beyond the entrance. Her fingers were locked together, and she held her shoulders inward as if expecting a blow. The pale blue dress she wore was so plain that the choice seemed calculated. Color had drained from her face, her eyes were inflamed, and the severe line of her mouth suggested that willpower alone was keeping her upright.
I had never seen her before.
My body distrusted her anyway. Kira surged with a warning growl, forcing me to clamp my teeth together before the sound escaped.
A prickle spread over my skin as apprehension twisted low in my abdomen. I tried to dismiss it as response to an uninvited stranger and nothing more.
At my side, Julian had become motionless.
There was no surprise in him and no uncertainty. He looked trapped in ice.
I searched his face. "Julian, what is it?"
Silence was his only answer.
The stranger edged farther into the hall. "I'm sorry," she began, her voice unsteady. "This is a terrible place to do it, and I won't take much of your time."
By then, nobody pretended not to stare. Interest sharpened the guests' expressions, and their attention traveled between the woman and me.
"I needed to tell you how sorry I am," she continued. "For leaving the way I did. For all of it."
Julian's throat worked as he forced down a swallow.
"Camille."
Her name came from him like a wound reopening.
So he knew this woman.
Whatever smile remained on my face disappeared.
"There wasn't another way I could manage," Camille said. "I've practiced this conversation a hundred times, but every version sounded wrong."
Her eyes darted toward me, measuring what she found.
"You deserve an apology too," she added, as though my existence had occurred to her late.
Cold pressure spread behind my breastbone.
I did not understand her regret, nor could I explain why Julian appeared close to breaking apart. I only knew that every instinct me rejected what was unfolding.
Whispers stirred somewhere behind my shoulder. Any ordinary human would have missed them beneath the music, but everyone in this room believed I was ordinary.
They were mistaken.
"It's really her."
"His fated mate."
"She's the twins' birth mother."
For several heartbeats, the phrases carried no meaning. My mind refused to accept them, letting each revelation pass through without taking hold.
Camille's composure began to fracture. "After the twins were born, I left. I was ill, and I couldn't function. Postpartum depression almost killed me."
The floor seemed to roll beneath my feet.
My gaze dropped toward the children's table without conscious thought. Oscar had abandoned his picture. Emily, no longer coloring, watched the adults with confusion pinching her brow.
My pulse battered against my throat.
"I didn't want to desert them," Camille said. "I just wasn't safe then, not for the babies and not for myself."
Postpartum.
That one word refused to move.
"I've been receiving treatment," she said. "I've recovered. I only came because I wanted to see them, even if I get one chance and nothing else."
Julian moved toward her.
His eyes never came to me.
"This conversation can't happen here," he said, keeping his voice low.
Relief softened Camille's features. At the same instant, pain twisted through my stomach with brutal force.
"I understand," she breathed. "I didn't know anywhere else I could find you."
"I'll arrange place for you tonight," Julian told her. "After that, we'll talk."
He spoke with certainty, as if the decision had already been made. My stomach plunged.
Tears escaped freely down her face as she nodded. "Thank you."
Julian turned toward the doors and began leading her out, one hand suspended protectively behind her without quite touching.
I remained where he had left me, still gripping the glass I had raised for him. The words of my own toast mocked me inside the sudden hollow of my head.
Surely, he would glance back.
He never did.
For one reckless moment, I nearly called after him. I wanted to block his path and force every explanation out of him before he took another step.
But an entire ballroom was waiting for my reaction.
Worse, the twins were waiting too.
I fell back on the skill that had carried me through every difficult year.
I adjusted.
When Oscar reached up, I crossed the room and gathered him against my body. Then I bent to press my lips into Emily's hair.
"Everything is fine," I told them softly. "You can finish your pictures."
Around us, the guests lingered in uncomfortable clusters, uncertain whether the celebration had ended.
I drew myself upright, ran a careful palm over my dress, and assembled pleasant expression.
"Please continue enjoying the party," I said. "My husband should be back with us soon."
Gratitude loosened the room. The music swelled again, and interrupted conversations restarted with forced enthusiasm.
Later, people would compliment my dignity. They would call me graceful.
I lifted my champagne once more, and my fingers remained perfectly steady.
"Here's to achievement," I said. "And here's to family."
The response came quieter than before.
I drank while staring at the doorway that had swallowed Julian and Camille. Somewhere beneath my practiced calm, certainty was already taking root: the joy that had filled me when the evening began had vanished for good.
I simply had not discovered its price yet.

Chapter 2: Left Behind
Avery POV
The banquet ended for Julian the instant he followed Camille out.
He never returned.
For a while, I invented excuses on his behalf. Camille had arrived overwhelmed. Julian only needed a few minutes to calm her down. Whatever had pulled him away involved the pack, and once it was handled, he would come back and explain everything.
Still smiling, I watched the door.
Five minutes slipped past. Then ten. By twenty, keeping my expression pleasant had become painful.
Something in my chest fractured with every additional second.
Eventually, the guests abandoned their performance of concern. Talk resumed around me, drifting toward business arrangements, wine, and the food on their plates. Laughter returned with an almost grateful volume. One person praised the dessert while someone else requested the recipe.
Whenever anyone addressed me, I nodded and supplied the expected response. The motions required no thought.
All my attention remained fixed on the doorway.
Then Emily scrubbed at her tired eyes, and Oscar began rocking where he stood. Exhaustion had finally defeated their curiosity. I couldn't leave them surrounded by whispers and artificial smiles any longer.
"I'll take the children upstairs," I told a guest nearby. Politeness held my voice together. "Please stay and enjoy the evening."
Nobody objected. Nobody even made an effort to.
With one child holding each hand, I crossed toward the packhouse's eastern wing and our apartment. Heavy doors swallowed the banquet noise behind us, leaving the corridor unusually quiet and cold.
Oscar dragged his feet like a tiny sleepwalker. His fingers barely curled around mine, and his chin dipped toward his chest every few steps. Emily moved with unnatural precision beside me, gripping my hand hard enough to hurt.
Just before we reached the stairs, her soft voice broke the silence.
"Mommy, who was that lady?"
Pain knotted my stomach.
Emily had always noticed far more than a child her age should. Adults concealed things; she observed the gaps, tucked them away, and waited until she was ready to ask.
She deserved honesty from me.
The problem was that I had no truth to offer.
When she raised her face, Julian's glacial blue eyes stared back at me. She had inherited his focus too, and now she expected me to explain the choices he refused to explain himself.
Without the banquet whispers, I would've known nothing at all. Julian hadn't looked at me before leaving with Camille. He had given me no word, gesture, or warning.
I shaped my mouth into what I hoped passed for reassurance.
"I'm not sure, Sweet Girl," I said. "She might be someone Daddy knew a long time ago."
Even spoken gently, the lie left bitterness on my tongue.
Emily came to a stop and studied me. Her gaze narrowed, searching for whatever I had withheld. Instead of challenging me, she made a quiet, doubtful hum.
Tears would've hurt less than that little sound.
Light spilled beneath our apartment door when we arrived.
I slowed before touching the handle.
There were people talking inside. Then Camille's uneven sobbing rose above the low voices.
I entered and stopped cold.
Beside the couch stood Julian, his body turned toward Camille while one hand moved steadily over her back. I knew that touch. The position of his palm, the measured pressure, the slow rhythm meant to bring someone back from grief. He had soothed me exactly that way whenever I cried.
Camille sat pressed close to him. Damp strands of long blonde hair veiled part of her face, and tears tracked from her reddened brown eyes while her full lips quivered.
Everything about her suggested delicacy.
Too much delicacy to be real.
Julian noticed me and turned his head. That single glance cleaved straight through my heart.
Nothing else about him shifted. His shoulders remained oriented toward Camille, and his hand stayed firmly against her back. His icy gaze skimmed over the children as if they were incidental, then returned to her.
"Camille is staying here," he announced before I could speak. His tone allowed neither debate nor hesitation. "She needs time to settle in."
I expected him to add, "with us."
The words never came.
I also waited for him to acknowledge Emily and Oscar. He failed to do that too.
Oscar sagged sleepily against my thigh. Emily's nails pressed crescents into my palm.
"For how long?" I asked.
Annoyance tightened Julian's face, as though my question itself were unreasonable. "For now."
An answer that explained nothing.
After one small nod, I said, "The kids need baths and bed. They're exhausted."
My voice sounded distant even to me, smooth because I had stripped every feeling out of it.
"Avery..." Julian began.
By then, I had already turned away.
Remaining in that room would've cost me whatever control I still possessed. I needed walls between us, space for my body and my thoughts, anything that might keep the pain from spreading farther.
Steam soon clouded the bathroom while the tub filled. The prospect of warm water briefly revived Oscar, but as soon as I lowered him into it, his eyelids began to droop.
Exactly what I'd expected.
Emily sat rigidly beside him with her knees drawn up. Usually, she filled every room with brightness. Tonight, that light had dimmed, leaving a storm gathered behind her eyes.
Crouching at the tub, I smoothed the wet hair away from her face.
"Hey," I whispered. "You're safe."
No response came.
Kira shifted inside me.
'Let me soothe her,' she offered gently.
I loosened my hold just enough for her presence to surface. A quiet warmth spread from me and softened the air, steady rather than forceful. Some of the tension left Emily's shoulders.
A faint smile touched my lips.
Within minutes, Oscar had fallen completely asleep.
I had just lifted him from the water and wrapped him in a towel when Camille appeared at the bathroom entrance.
From this close, her perfection felt calculated. The ends of her blonde hair were wet and stuck to her shoulders. Crying had left her eyes swollen and her lips puffy. She glanced at Emily, then quickly focused on me.
"Could you use some help?" she asked while dabbing at her eyes.
Her sweetness sounded measured, each word carefully selected.
Before I could refuse, Emily jerked her head from side to side.
"No."
Camille's smile pinched at the corners. "I can lift you out," she said, moving toward the tub without permission.
Fear sharpened Emily's second refusal. "No!"
Her reaction made perfect sense.
Until this evening, Camille had never existed in my daughter's life. She was a stranger who had entered our home without warning, and no one had bothered to tell Emily why.
I placed Oscar on the padded bench and carefully dressed him in his pajamas.
"I can manage," I told Camille, keeping each word civil and restrained. "There's nothing you need to do."
Her mouth flattened into a narrow, cutting curve.
Then, ignoring me, she reached into the tub.
Both hands clamped around Emily's shoulders. The grip was forceful, demanding.
Emily recoiled.
"Stop! Let me go!" Panic shook her voice.
I spun toward them. "Take your hands off my daughter."
The command escaped before caution could soften it.
But Emily was mine.
I had fed her and rocked her through nightmares. Every illness, every burst of laughter, and every tear had found me beside her. I had never failed to come when she needed someone.
A choked noise came from Camille.
"She isn't your daughter," she hissed.
The wounded mask vanished. Cold possession replaced it, stark and vicious in her eyes.
"Yes, I am!" Emily shrieked.
Terror gave her enough strength to wrench herself loose. Her wet body twisted, her foot lost its purchase, and she fell.
Her skull hit the tub's edge with a hard, nauseating crack.
Red immediately streaked her skin.
Oscar jolted awake and screamed.
Crying out, Emily covered the wound with both hands. Blood pushed between her small fingers.
For one impossible beat, my heart seemed to quit moving.
Julian charged into the bathroom.
At once, Camille let go and threw herself backward. She covered her face as sobs overtook her. "She attacked me," she wailed.
Julian's gaze never went to Emily.
His daughter was bleeding from the temple, yet he didn't kneel, inspect the injury, or even ask if she was all right.
Instead, he faced me.
"What have you done?" The accusation in his voice cut sharper than the question.
What the fuck was happening?
"Camille grabbed her," I said. Already on my knees, I pressed a towel against Emily's head. My hands had begun to tremble. "She frightened Emily, and then she slipped."
"You're lying," Julian snapped.
Through her sobs, Emily fought to speak. "Daddy, she grabbed..."
"That's enough," he said, silencing her.
Not even then did he look at his child.
His expression turned glacial. "You're a liar. Avery has taught you to be one."
The words landed harder than any open-handed blow.
Whatever remained intact inside me finally gave way.
I offered no defense. I didn't shout or demand that he see what was in front of him.
My attention narrowed to Emily beneath my hands, Oscar clutching my leg, and the widening stain soaking through the towel.
So I gathered both children close and said nothing.
One person in that room had to keep them safe.
Julian had made it brutally clear that person would never be him.

Chapter 3: The Cold Side

Avery POV
The space beside me was empty when I opened my eyes.
For a moment, that seemed ordinary. Work sometimes drove Julian out of bed before dawn, and I could imagine him downstairs with coffee, trying to solve whatever problem had followed him home. Still half asleep, I remained under the covers and listened for him.
Silence pressed against the bedroom.
No water rushed through the shower pipes. The floorboards didn't creak beneath his steps, and nothing clinked in the kitchen. The twins weren't making any noise either, so they had to be asleep.
I touched Julian's side of the mattress.
The sheets weren't merely cool from a recent departure. They held the deep chill of a bed left vacant for hours.
Tension wound through my chest.
The clock showed a few minutes past seven. Sitting up, I let the sheet slide from my legs and stared at the untouched pillow. Even after a bad night, he should have returned by now.
Restlessness rippled through Kira.
'He never came back,' she said inside my mind, her voice quiet but watchful.
'I've noticed.'
I slipped into my robe and headed downstairs.
Julian lay unconscious on the sofa.
Yesterday's clothes still covered him. His jacket had been placed neatly across the armrest, as though someone had taken care not to wrinkle it. One shoe remained on his foot while the other rested on the floor. Bent into an uncomfortable sprawl, he looked as if exhaustion had dropped him in the first place he'd found.
Concern moved through me before I could prevent it. My hand almost reached for his tangled curls, but the memory of everything I'd felt yesterday stopped me.
Then movement in the kitchen caught my eye.
Camille was standing in MY kitchen with the ease of someone who lived there. The sheer fucking audacity of it made my skin prickle.
She had bare feet and a relaxed posture. Both hands curved around MY mug, the one decorated with pink glitter and the words "best mommy." Without pausing to search, she crossed from the stove to the counter, opened the correct drawers, and selected utensils as if familiarity entitled her to them.
Nothing needed to be explained to her.
Pain shot through my jaw from how tightly I locked my teeth.
My home.
My kitchen.
The life I had built.
Until yesterday, none of it had been in question. Now she was settling into every corner, quietly laying claim to what belonged to me.
Kira surged closer to the surface. 'Give us 5 seconds. That's all we'd need.'
'And what happens afterward?'
When I moved forward, my toes grazed the rug.
The faint sound jolted Julian awake.
Confusion clouded his face as he blinked at the room. Then his gaze found mine, and relief softened his expression. "Avery. You're awake."
"Clearly," I said. "Looks like I have company."
The words barely rose above a mutter, but the slight break in his gaze told me his wolf had probably heard them.
He pushed himself upright, worked the stiffness from his shoulders, and approached me. I didn't move. Waiting for him was automatic after six years together.
His lips touched my cheek.
Only there.
There was no kiss on my mouth, no lingering warmth, nothing intimate or familiar. He gave me a brief, courteous peck, the sort exchanged by people who barely knew each other.
The sensation in my stomach was like stepping onto a stair that wasn't there.
Less than a day ago, his mouth had stayed on mine. He'd held me against him, unhurried, his palms warm on my back. He had carried me to our bed over his shoulder and claimed my body three times, pulling me close each time as if separation were unbearable.
This morning, I received a token acknowledgment before he moved on.
Kira shrank back in disgust.
I hadn't found my voice when Camille faced us.
Her attention fixed immediately on Julian's mouth, then shifted to the place on my cheek he'd kissed.
Her expression crumpled.
Nothing about it was restrained or spontaneous. Her shoulders collapsed, her lips quivered, and moisture appeared in her eyes with the precision of a rehearsed performance.
"Oh," she breathed.
Every muscle in Julian's body went still.
He withdrew from me at once. The angle of his body changed, creating space between us with the speed of an instinctive response.
"Camille." Strain tightened his voice.
She hurriedly shook her head. "No, don't worry. It's fine. I shouldn't have... I never meant to..."
Turning away, she squeezed the mug as if it were the only thing keeping her upright.
In one practiced instant, she became the center of the room.
Julian went to her before he seemed aware he'd moved. He eased the mug from her grip, placed it on the counter, and reached for a second cup that had already been prepared.
That one was for him.
"I remembered how you take it," she murmured.
He accepted the drink.
His eyes never came back to me.
Heat knotted beneath my ribs, vicious and immediate. It hadn't become heartbreak yet.
It was rage.
Clean, bright, cutting rage.
Kira prowled through my mind with a low growl. I seriously considered exposing what we were just to teach that skank to keep her hands, manufactured drama, and fake boobs away from my family.
Folding my arms, I drove my nails into my skin.
"Comfortable night?" I asked him.
Julian flinched as though my voice had reminded him I was still present.
"Not exactly. I stayed down here because I didn't want to disturb you."
It wasn't the truth, or it wasn't all of it.
Camille delicately cleared her throat. "I can go upstairs. I don't want to be in the way."
"No." His answer came instantly, far too quickly. "Stay. You're fine."
You're fine.
Those two words seemed to fill the kitchen.
Camille compressed her lips, performing another attempt at restraint. Perhaps she was suppressing a smile. Perhaps it was triumph. Bitch.
At last, Julian turned and gave me his full attention.
He rubbed his neck. "Avery, I've been thinking. We need to explain this to the kids."
I said nothing.
"They should understand who Camille is," he went on.
My heartbeat lurched. Of course the twins deserved an explanation about who the fuck this stranger was. But I deserved one too, didn't I? He still hadn't shown enough decency to sit with me and explain any part of this disaster. He had hardly spoken to me at all.
"When exactly were you going to explain it to me?"
His eyes blinked once.
Only then did comprehension reach him.
Alarm spread across his face, arriving far too late. "Oh. Avery, I... I should have talked to you sooner. I wasn't trying to..."
Trying to do what?
Make me disappear?
"I forgot," he finished, and even he seemed to hear how pathetic that sounded. "It all happened too quickly. Emily last night, then Camille arriving... There's a lot to deal with."
A lot for him, apparently.
Nothing for me.
"I'm overwhelmed," he added softly, offering the admission as if it answered everything.
Then, before I could respond, more words poured out of him. He always kept talking when pressure closed in.
"Maybe we should get the twins out of the house today. They could use some air, and we could do something ordinary. Maybe have a picnic."
A picnic.
"We?"
Surely, he didn't mean what I feared. We had to mean Julian and me. He couldn't intend to take our children, without warning, on an outing with the woman who had abandoned them. He wouldn't shut me out of it. Would he?
His pause answered before he did.
"Camille and me," he said. "It might be easier if you stay home. They need some time to bond with their mother."
The sentence struck harder than an open hand.
I could only stare.
"I'm their mother."
"Yes." Relief briefly lit his face, as if I had finally understood his reasoning. "Of course you are, honey. But they also have to meet their other mom."
Mom.
Fire spread through my chest, and this wasn't some figure of speech. Every breath physically hurt.
I gave him time to hear himself, retract the words, or find some way to include me.
He did none of those things.
Kira's snarl rang through my skull.
I forced down the pressure in my throat before answering.
"I'm not feeling well, so it doesn't matter. Enjoy yourselves."
A crease formed between his eyebrows. "You're sure you aren't angry?"
"Yes."
Angry was far too small a word for what had started consuming me.
I headed for the door. Air wasn't enough. I wanted to cross into rogue territory, tear away my clothes, and surrender control to Kira.
With my hand on the doorway, I spoke without turning. "Oscar is allergic to nuts, including trace amounts. And Emily can't have dairy first thing in the morning."
Camille nodded eagerly. "I know. Of course I do."
Before my mouth could expose everything boiling inside me, I seized my coat and walked out.
Winter air scorched my lungs. I drove myself forward without choosing a destination, caring only about putting more ground between me and that house.
By the time I passed the tree line, Kira was completely awake.
She wasn't frantic anymore, and she wasn't raging. Her presence had become something dense and steady within my bones.
I couldn't have said how long we ran.
We kept moving until strain replaced the ache in my muscles. Kira took control and ripped through the brush, hunting with no restraint. Rabbit after rabbit fell to her. There were more than I could count, far beyond hunger or need.
When I finally returned to my human body, emotion had been scraped out of me. The anger was gone. So were the jealousy and the keen edge of hatred.
Only a hollow space remained.
My fingers had gone numb as I dressed. The journey home took longer, each step weighed down by heavy legs. Worse than the earlier fury was the unnatural stillness inside my head.
When I returned, no one was there.
The silence felt absolute.
The twins weren't laughing or bickering over some meaningless offense. No voices traveled from another room. Stale, undisturbed air filled the house.
Julian had actually taken my children to have a picnic with that woman, leaving me behind.
I stopped in the entryway with my keys clenched in one hand and stared at a point that didn't exist.
My phone began to ring.
At first, I didn't check the display.
There was no need.
After years spent at the edge of pack life, never truly part of it, I knew that number by heart. It belonged to the pack's hospital.
The emptiness inside me tightened into dread.
I answered the call.
"Avery?" The woman on the line maintained a professional tone, but urgency strained every word. "I'm calling from Silver Moon Medical. You need to come here immediately."
Feeling crashed back into me all at once.
"What happened?"
Her silence lasted a fraction too long.
"It's Oscar. He's having a severe allergic reaction. We've stabilized him for the moment, but..."
Whatever followed never reached me.
My hand had already started trembling. I snatched up my keys again while my heart battered my ribs.
"How did this happen?" Even to my own ears, my voice came from somewhere far away.
"We're still determining that," she said with measured caution. "But he ingested something he shouldn't have."

Room 17.

I had fucking warned her.

Julian.

"I have a call to deal with," he said, his tone suddenly sharp as he drew the phone from his pocket.
He aimed one last irritated glance at me before disappearing through the doorway.
Carefully, I lowered myself onto the edge of Oscar's mattress. I kept hold of him, terrified that releasing his hand might disturb the fragile balance keeping him safe. Emily wedged herself beneath my arm, her shoulder pressed firmly into my side.
The machines continued their soft, measured beeping. They carried on without concern while something inside our family fractured beyond any repair I could imagine.
Silence held us for a long while.
Eventually, Oscar shifted against the pillows.
"I didn't eat the sandwich," he said. His voice remained frail, though I could understand every word. "I smelled it before I took a bite."
My throat constricted.
"What did you smell?" I asked, smoothing all emotion from my tone for his sake.
"Peanut butter. I told her it smelled wrong, but she said I could eat it."
I dipped my head, acknowledging the answer while something cold settled through me.
Beside me, Emily went rigid.
"She wouldn't let me use the ball," she murmured. Her words were almost too quiet to hear. "She told me soccer isn't for girls."
My eyelids fell shut.
Only for a moment.
When I looked again, the room had blurred around its edges. I swallowed against the ache in my chest and made myself draw one steady breath after another.
"Neither of you did anything wrong." I turned so they could both see my face. "Not one thing. Do you understand me? None of this belongs to you."
Emily folded against me, resting her forehead on my arm the way she had when she was younger.
"You're our mom," she said. "She isn't."
That broke the last of my defenses.
I curved one arm around Emily and drew her close while keeping Oscar's hand inside mine. I held them both as tightly as I safely could, wishing my body were enough to barricade them from everything that might cause them pain.
Oscar let his head drift toward my shoulder. His fingers remained woven through mine.
"I know," I managed, my voice scraped raw. "I know, baby."
After that, time lost its shape.
Doctors entered, examined Oscar, and left again. Nurses altered the monitors, recorded his vital signs, and offered reassurance in carefully lowered voices. Their explanations barely reached me.
Instead, I tracked every change myself: Oscar's breaths becoming smoother, the angry rash retreating from his skin, warmth and color gradually returning to his face.
Not once did I release his hand.
Julian never returned.
Camille stayed away as well.
At last, the doctor declared Oscar stable and gave us permission to take him home. Relief struck with enough force to set my hands trembling again.
It wasn't joy.
Gratitude didn't describe it, either.
The feeling was pure release after hours spent braced for disaster.
I helped Oscar out of the hospital gown and into his clothes. When his weakened legs failed beneath him, I lifted him against my chest. His weight settled naturally into my arms, exactly where he belonged.
Emily remained attached to my side. Her fingers hooked through my jacket sleeve, and she showed no intention of letting go.
No one spoke during the drive home. By the time the packhouse appeared, exhaustion had hollowed me out, and all I wanted was to collapse onto a bed.
Fear, fury, and adrenaline had churned my thoughts into chaos. Worse, they had made containing Kira nearly impossible.
I wound my mother's necklace around my fingers. She had given it to me shortly before she passed away, and for several dangerous seconds, I considered removing it. Without its restraint, Camille would finally understand exactly who she had chosen to provoke.
But unleashing Kira wouldn't help my pups.
That truth kept the necklace in place.
Silence greeted us inside the packhouse, although every light in our apartment had been switched on.
I crossed the entryway, then stopped.
Adelaide stood in the living room with her back facing us. Julian's mother - my mother-in-law - had clasped two hands between her own, joining them with the reverence of someone displaying a sacred bond.
One hand belonged to Julian.
The other was Camille's.
"This is what should have happened from the beginning," Adelaide said, certainty warming her voice. "You two belong together. Fate doesn't make errors."
My stomach plunged.
Julian made no attempt to free himself. Instead, he drew a measured breath, almost as if he were preparing to receive some holy gift.
Then he met Camille's eyes.
A smile touched his face, and he nodded.
"No," he agreed. "Fate doesn't."
No. Apparently it didn't.

Chapter 5: The Breaking Point
Avery POV
Oscar's arms cinched around my neck when he shifted against my hip. Exhaustion still weighed on him, and weakness had not released its grip, yet he clung with a child's fierce certainty that loosening his hold might make someone carry him away. Supporting his back with one hand, I eased him higher without jarring him.
Beside me, Emily threaded her fingers more tightly through mine. She leaned into my leg, trying to become a barrier between me and whatever danger she thought was waiting in the room. Lately, she had been doing that more and more.
No child should have developed that reflex so early, even one born an alpha like me.
On the other side of the room, Camille's hand remained enclosed in Julian's.
Nothing theatrical passed between them. Their fingers did not tighten, and neither of them exchanged a loaded glance. Julian simply kept holding on, as though the possibility of releasing her had never entered his mind.
A furious outburst would have hurt less.
At least anger would have meant he saw me.
I moved one step into the room.
That small motion finally drew their attention. Something flashed through Julian's eyes, perhaps guilt or shame, before his expression hardened. He put on the cold mask he had never worn for me before, the same one that had earned him the nickname "icy boss" among his human staff.
"Sorry to intrude on the reunion," I said. My tone remained remarkably even, without a tremor to betray me. I could have been discussing an ordinary change in the weather. "I came to tell you that Oscar is stable and has been discharged. Clearly, he's right here."
To underline the point, I lifted him a little.
A bitter thought pressed at the back of my mind: as though any of you care. I buried it before it could reach my face. This was neither the time nor the place, especially with my children watching.
For an instant, Adelaide's features pinched as she faced me. Then the tension vanished beneath a polished expression of concern. Over the years, she had perfected the art of wrapping condemnation in apparent kindness.
"Thank goodness Oscar is recovering," she said with practiced warmth. "We were terribly concerned."
Only then did I notice her husband. Alpha Malcolm sat on our sofa with a bourbon in hand, calmly occupying our home as if he belonged there.
Adelaide inspected the faint line the oxygen tube had left on Oscar's skin. Her attention soon returned to Julian, where it lingered longer than necessary.
"We came the moment we found out."
Of course they had.
Discomfort finally touched Camille's face. Remembering, perhaps, that appearances mattered, she relaxed her hold on Julian by a fraction. Still, she did not release him.
I refused to give her my attention.
Julian was the one I watched.
"We need to talk," I said.
He waited a beat too long before noding. I noticed the hesitation, however slight. "What is there to discuss?"
Everything.
Our son had almost died that day. Julian had accused me without pausing to think. When Camille needed protection, he had placed himself between us as though she might shatter and I was the weapon threatening to break her.
None of that left my mouth.
"What happens from here," I said instead.
A heavy quiet settled over everyone.
Adelaide's smile narrowed. "Avery, this is hardly the appropriate moment." Her gentle delivery carried the patronizing patience reserved for someone whose objections had already been dismissed.
"There won't be a better one."
My voice stayed low, and I never turned toward her. Julian remained fixed in my sights.
First, he looked at Malcolm. Next came Adelaide. His final glance went to Camille.
No answer followed.
His refusal to speak revealed more than an admission ever could.
Irritation broke through Adelaide's composure, lifting her eyebrows. "You are behaving irrationaly."
"No, I'm reacting like a person," I snapped. "Our son suffered an allergic reaction serious enough to put him in the hospital. I warned Camille, and I left clear instructions. This is about his safety, not some private grudge."
Right on cue, Camille's bottom lip began to quiver. "He isn't your child! Besides, I already apologized. I never intended to-"
"Stop," Julian cut in sharply.
Hope flared inside me for one humiliating second. It was instinct rather than reason, a remnant of the faith I had once placed in him. Some part of me still expected him to return to the role he had abandoned.
Then his attention swung toward me.
"You've taken this too far, Avery. Everyone is worn out, and emotions are running high. You're making the situation bigger than it has to be." His expression did not soften. "We have nothing to discuss."
I could only stare.
Out of every possible response, that was his choice.
"Is Camille going to stay here?" I asked again.
This time, I needed a direct answer. I needed to hear him confirm that he would allow the woman who had deserted him and his children six years earlier to force her way back into their lives. I needed to witness him placing the wreckage of their mate bond above his own children.
He had already chosen her over me. Emily and Oscar, however, deserved better. They deserved a mother who would never feed them peanut butter while insisting it was safe. They deserved someone who would not bar them from soccer because of their gender.
Julian dragged a hand down his face and released a slow breath. "She has nowhere else to go right now."
He had offered an excuse, not answer.
Circumstance made a convenient disguise for a lie.
"Then if she remains here, I won't," I said. My pulse hammered against my ribs, but none of it entered my voice.
Emily sucked in a sharp breath.
Her nails bit into my skin as she gripped my hand.
"No." She pressed even closer to me. "I'm leaving too. I won't stay here without you."
Julian jerked his head up. "Emily-"
"I don't want Camille in this house," she said, raising her voice over him. Though each word trembled, she held her ground. "She frightens me."
Oscar stirred against my shoulder and weakly raised his head. Confusion creased his forehead before sadness overtook it.
"She scares me too," he whispered.
Everyone went still.
Adelaide started to respond, but no sound emerged. Her mouth closed again. She plainly had not expected either child to reject Camille.
Shock crossed Julian's face, followed by embarrassment. He looked trapped.
Camille rocked on her feet and brought one hand to her chest.
"Everything is spinning," she murmured. "I think... I think I have to sit down."
Julian reacted at once. With his palm braced securely against her back, he stered her toward the couch. "Sit before you fall. You can't overexert yourself."
Until then, Alpha Malcolm had remained silent.
"Julian," he said in a measured voice, "it may be wise to have her examined. Better to be cautious."
And there it was: permission.
Julian agreed without hesitation. "You're right. That's probably best."
He spoke without once looking in my direction.

bodyText:
I almost went down in front of the whole congregation on Easter Sunday.

Right there in the center aisle. Third pew from the front. Communion tray in my hands.

I remember the moment my knees started to buckle. The way the sanctuary tilted just a little to the left, like somebody had bumped the whole building. The stained glass window behind the pulpit went from a bright red cross to a smear of pink. I heard Pastor Whitfield say something about the blood of the lamb but his voice sounded like it was coming from under water.

I gripped the back of the pew. Real tight. My knuckles went ashy.

Sister Loretta was next to me. She grabbed my elbow without even looking at me, the way women in that church have been catching each other for 60 years. Nobody else saw. Or if they did, they had the grace to pretend they didn't.

I sat down. Passed the tray on. Kept my head bowed like I was praying so nobody would see the sweat on my upper lip.

I got through the rest of the service. I got through the potluck in the fellowship hall. I got in my car in the parking lot behind the church and I sat there for 20 minutes before I could trust myself to drive home.

That was seven months ago.

The christening is in four weeks.

My granddaughter Amara. Six months old. My daughter Jasmine's first baby. First grandbaby on both sides of the family. And Jasmine has been planning this christening since before Amara was born, picking out the little white dress, ordering the programs, telling everybody in Tuscaloosa to save the date.

And I have been laying awake at night trying to figure out how to tell my only daughter that I can't stand up in front of that congregation and hold her baby over the baptismal font without going down.

My name is DeShawna. I'm 54 years old. I've been the church secretary at First African Baptist here in Tuscaloosa for 16 years.

That means I know every family in that congregation. I know whose grandmama is in hospice. I know who just made deacon. I know which teenagers are on the prayer list and which ones we're just praying about quietly. I type the bulletins on Thursday nights. I put the flowers on the altar Saturday mornings. I unlock the office at 7:30 AM Monday through Friday and I lock it back up at 4:30.

That church is my second home. My husband Marcus says it's my first home and our house on 22nd Avenue is my second, and he's not exactly wrong.

Marcus works at the construction supply place off McFarland Boulevard. Has for 31 years. We raised two kids in a three bedroom brick ranch. Jasmine is 27, works for the school system, just had Amara last April. Our son Kendrick is 24 and lives out in Birmingham working for a bank.

I have been blessed. I know that. I say that every morning before my feet hit the floor.

But two years ago something started going wrong with my body and I have not been able to figure out how to fix it.

It started with the dizziness.

Just here and there at first. I'd stand up too fast from my desk and I'd have to grab the file cabinet. I'd bend down to pick up a bulletin somebody dropped and when I stood back up the room would swim for a second.

I told my doctor. Dr. Patel over at the medical office on Hackberry Lane. Sweet man. Kind eyes. Been my doctor for 12 years.

He took my blood pressure. Frowned. Took it again. Frowned deeper.

"DeShawna. This is 168 over 102. When did this start?"

I told him I didn't know. I hadn't been checking. I thought high blood pressure was something old people had. I was 52.

He put me on a pill. Little white one. Take one every morning with breakfast.

I took it. Every morning. With breakfast.

Three months later my pressure was 162 over 98.

He added a second pill. Slightly bigger. Take it at night.

I took it. Every night.

Three months after that my pressure was 156 over 96.

He increased the dose on the first one. Told me to cut out salt. Told me to lose 20 pounds. Told me stress was probably part of it and had I thought about maybe doing yoga.

I did not do yoga. I did not have time to do yoga. I was working 40 hours a week at the church and helping Jasmine set up her nursery and my mother in Bessemer had just been diagnosed with something the doctors couldn't quite name yet.

But I cut the salt. I stopped putting it on my eggs. I stopped adding it to my greens. Marcus complained about the greens. I told Marcus to hush.

I lost 8 pounds. My pressure came down 4 points.

The dizziness kept getting worse.

Then came the headaches.

The kind that start at the base of your skull and creep up over the top of your head like a hot washcloth being pulled tight. I'd get them at my desk around 2 in the afternoon. I'd get them driving home. I'd get them in the middle of the night and wake up with my pillow damp from the sweat.

I started keeping a bottle of Tylenol in my purse. Then one in my desk drawer. Then one in the glove box.

Marcus noticed. He notices everything, even when he pretends he doesn't. One night he came into the bathroom while I was shaking two more tablets into my palm and he said, "Baby. That's the fourth time today."

I said I was fine.

He said, "You're not fine."

I said, "I said I'm fine, Marcus."

He didn't push. That's not his way. But I saw him put the bottle back in the cabinet slow, the way you handle a thing you're worried about.

The Easter Sunday thing was the worst of it. But it wasn't the only time.

I nearly went down again at the Piggly Wiggly reaching for a bag of rice on the bottom shelf. I nearly went down in the church office standing up from my chair to answer the door. I nearly went down at my mother's bedside in Bessemer trying to help her get to the bathroom.

Every time, I'd catch myself. Grab something. Sit down. Breathe.

Every time, I'd tell myself it was fine.

Every time, I'd think about the fact that both my grandmothers had strokes. My daddy's mama died of one at 61. My mama's mama had one at 66 and lived another eight years but never walked right again.

I'm 54.

I did the math on the drive to work every morning. I did it while I was making Marcus's coffee. I did it while I was sitting at the church office typing up the visitation list.

Every prayer I said started the same way. Please Lord. Just let me get to Amara's christening. Just let me hold that baby over the water.

That's all I want.

Jasmine called me on a Wednesday night about three months after Amara was born. She was crying.

Not sad crying. Happy crying. The kind of crying my daughter does when she's got something big to tell you and she can't get the words out.

"Mama. Mama, listen. Pastor Whitfield said yes. October 18th. We can do it October 18th."

The christening. She'd been going back and forth with the church about the date for weeks.

October 18th was 10 weeks away.

She kept talking. About the dress. About the reception at her house after. About whether I thought Aunt Regina would fly in from Detroit or if we should Facetime her in. About whether Marcus wanted to read a scripture. About whether I'd hold Amara during the actual ceremony because Jasmine's hands would be shaking too bad.

I sat on the edge of my bed with the phone pressed to my ear and I said "of course baby, of course" and I smiled with my voice because that's what mamas do.

I hung up. I looked at Marcus. He was in his chair reading the paper.

I said, "I don't know if I can do it."

He put the paper down.

He said, "DeShawna. Come here."

I went and sat next to him. He put his arm around me. He smelled like the Old Spice he's been wearing since 1992.

He said, "Baby. What's going on."

And I told him. The dizziness. The Easter Sunday thing. The Piggly Wiggly. The Tylenol. The math I was doing about my grandmothers. All of it. Everything I'd been carrying by myself for two years because I didn't want him to worry and I didn't want Jasmine to know and I didn't want anybody at the church to see me as anything other than the woman who unlocks the door at 7:30.

He held me while I cried.

Then he said, "We're going to figure this out. Together. But you have got to stop pretending."

I went back to Dr. Patel. He was kind about it. He always is.

He looked at my chart. He looked at me over the top of his glasses.

He said, "DeShawna, I want to be honest with you. We're doing what we can with these medications. But your numbers aren't where they need to be. We may need to add a third medication. And I need you to understand, at 54, with your family history, this is something we need to take very seriously."

He said the word stroke. Right out loud. I heard it and I felt my whole face get hot.

He said, "I'm not trying to scare you. I'm trying to be straight with you."

I nodded. I told him I appreciated it. I told him I'd do whatever he said.

He wrote me a new prescription. Third pill. Take it in the morning with the first one.

I filled it at the Walgreens on 15th Street on the way home. I put it in the cabinet with the other two.

I stood in front of the bathroom mirror that night and I looked at myself and I thought, I am 54 years old and I am on three blood pressure medications and I still feel like I might drop dead at my granddaughter's christening.

Something has to give.

The next Sunday after service I stayed behind in the fellowship hall.

Everybody else was outside in the parking lot doing what Baptists do after service, which is stand around talking for another 45 minutes when the service already ran long. I told Marcus I'd be out in a minute. I sat down at one of the folding tables with a paper plate of cornbread I wasn't going to eat.

Miss Ernestine came and sat next to me.

Miss Ernestine is 71. She's been the head deaconess at First African for longer than I've been the secretary. She's got short salt and pepper hair that she keeps in tight curls, and she wears reading glasses on a beaded chain around her neck, and she carries herself like a woman who has seen a whole lot and is not particularly impressed by any of it.

Before she retired, she was a labor and delivery nurse at DCH Regional Medical Center for 39 years. She delivered half the babies in this church. She probably delivered me, come to think of it, though I've never asked.

She sat down across from me. Didn't say anything for a minute. Just watched me not eat my cornbread.

Then she said, "Sister DeShawna. How long?"

I said, "How long what?"

She said, "How long have you been sitting down at the top of the stairs before you go up. How long have you been holding onto the pew when you stand for the doxology. How long have you been walking to the office instead of driving because you're scared you'll pass out at a red light."

I stared at her.

She said, "Baby. I was a nurse for 39 years. I see everything."

I started crying right there at the table with the cornbread in front of me.

Miss Ernestine did not hug me. Miss Ernestine is not a hugger.

She reached across the table and put her hand on top of mine. Her hand was warm and dry and covered in fine wrinkles and had two big rings on it, one wedding band and one that used to belong to her mother.

She said, "Tell me everything."

So I did. Right there in the fellowship hall while the rest of the church was outside. The dizziness. The three medications. Dr. Patel. My grandmothers. The christening. All of it.

She listened. Really listened. She did not interrupt. She did not offer solutions. She did not say "I know just how you feel."

When I was done she was quiet for a long time.

Then she said, "Come to my house Tuesday afternoon. 2 o'clock. I want to talk to you about something."

Miss Ernestine lives in a little brick house over in Alberta City. Marcus dropped me off on his way to work on Tuesday and I told him I'd call him when I was done.

She had sweet tea and a plate of Nilla wafers on the coffee table. That's Miss Ernestine's way. She feeds you before she talks to you.

She sat in her chair. I sat on her couch. Between us on the coffee table she'd laid out three things. A little brown bottle. A book with a green cover. And a printout of some kind, folded in half.

She said, "DeShawna. What did Dr. Patel tell you about why your pressure is high?"

I said, "He said it's genetic. And that I need to lose weight and reduce salt."

She said, "That's what he told you the cause is. But did he ever tell you what's actually happening inside your blood vessels?"

I said no. He hadn't.

She said, "Let me tell you what I learned in 39 years at DCH. Some of it from the cardiologists. Some of it from paying attention. And some of it from what I started reading after my husband Cleveland passed."

She unfolded the printout. It was some kind of article. She didn't hand it to me. She just kept talking.

"Your blood vessels aren't just tubes, DeShawna. They're alive. The inside of every artery in your body is lined with a layer of living cells. It's called the endothelium. It's not something they teach you in high school biology. But it's the most important thing in your whole cardiovascular system."

"Those cells have a job. Their job is to keep your vessels relaxed and open. They do that by producing a molecule called nitric oxide. When those cells are healthy, they make plenty of nitric oxide, and your vessels stay soft and flexible and open. Blood flows through easy. Pressure stays low."

"But those cells get worn down. By years of processed food. By stress. By inflammation. By pollution. By just living a long time in a hard world."

"When they get worn down, they can't make as much nitric oxide anymore. And when they can't make nitric oxide, your vessels stay tight. Blood has to force its way through. That's what high pressure is. It's not really a problem of too much blood. It's a problem of tubes that won't open."

I was leaning forward on the couch.

She said, "Now here's what they don't tell you at the doctor's office. Your medications don't fix the wall. They can't. What they do is force your vessels open from the outside. Which is fine. It brings the number down. But the wall keeps getting worse. Every year that goes by, the cells that line those arteries are more worn down than the year before. Which is why you keep needing more medication. And why the pressure keeps creeping back up."

She looked at me over her glasses.

"You are not failing your treatment, DeShawna. Your treatment isn't addressing what's actually broken."

I sat there with my tea getting warm in my hand.

She said, "About four years ago, after Cleveland passed and I retired, I started reading everything I could find on this. I lost him to a stroke, you know. He was 74. His pressure had been managed for 20 years. His numbers looked fine. And he still had a stroke. I could not let that go. I had to understand why."

"And what I kept coming back to was this endothelial wall. If you don't support the wall, you're always fighting the symptom and never touching the cause."

She picked up the little brown bottle. Handed it to me.

I turned it in my hand. The label said Auniva. Underneath that, in smaller letters, it said Amla.

I said, "What is this?"

She said, "Amla. It's a fruit. Grows on a tree in India. They call it the Indian gooseberry. It's been used in traditional medicine for thousands of years, but that's not why I take it. I take it because of what the research says about a group of compounds in it called emblicanins."

"Emblicanins have been studied for what they do to that endothelial wall. They help support those cells. When the wall is better supported, those cells can start producing more nitric oxide on their own. Not from the outside. Not forced. On their own. The way they did when you were younger."

"And when the wall makes its own nitric oxide again, vessels can relax more naturally. Blood can flow easier. Pressure can ease. Not because something forced it. Because your body started doing what it already knows how to do."

She paused.

"You have to support the wall first. Everything else is downstream of that."

I sat there for a long minute.

I thought about all the money I had spent on medications that were not doing what I needed them to do.

I thought about my grandmothers.

I thought about Amara.

I said, "Miss Ernestine. Can I be honest with you? I've tried supplements before. I took a fish oil for two years. My daughter got me on some magnesium. I did the garlic pills. Nothing did anything."

She smiled a small smile.

She said, "I know. I did all of those too. And I'll tell you why they didn't do what you needed them to do."

"Fish oil is fine. It's got its place. But it doesn't touch the wall. Neither does magnesium. Neither does garlic. Beetroot juice, that's a big one right now, all it does is dump nitric oxide into your system from the outside. Which is like pouring water into a bucket with a hole in it. Your body already knows how to make nitric oxide. That was never the problem. The problem was the wall was too worn out to make it."

"Amla is the only thing I've come across that goes to the wall. That's why it made a difference for me when nothing else did."

She rolled up her sleeve. She held out her forearm.

She said, "Take my pulse."

I put two fingers on her wrist the way she taught the deaconess board to do it when we did the CPR training three years ago. Her pulse was slow and steady and even.

She said, "I was on two blood pressure medications when Cleveland died. I've been off both of them for two and a half years. My last reading at Dr. Owens's office was 118 over 76. I take this and I take a walk around the block every morning and that is the entire program."

I did not decide right there at Miss Ernestine's coffee table.

I am not that kind of woman. I sit with things.

I went home. I told Marcus. He listened the way he listens, which is with his whole body. He looked at the bottle. He looked at me.

He said, "Baby. You've been on three of Dr. Patel's pills for four months and your pressure is still 154 over 92. What is there to lose."

I said, "It's $60."

He said, "Sixty dollars. DeShawna. We spent 60 dollars on that ridiculous pizza last Friday from that place on Skyland."

I laughed. First time I'd laughed in weeks.

He said, "It's got a 90 day money back thing. Miss Ernestine told you. If it doesn't do anything you send it back and you get your money. But you don't try, and that christening is going to come and go and you are going to have spent 10 weeks scared out of your mind."

I sat with that.

I ordered it that night. From the website Miss Ernestine wrote down for me on the back of a church bulletin. Two capsules a day. Free shipping. Made right here in the USA. It came in three days in a plain box on the porch.

I started the Wednesday it arrived. Two capsules with breakfast. I didn't stop any of my medications. I wasn't about to do anything stupid. Dr. Patel didn't know I was taking it. Nobody knew except Marcus and Miss Ernestine.

The first week I didn't feel anything different. I checked my pressure every morning on the little cuff Marcus bought me from CVS. Same numbers as before. 152 over 91. 155 over 93. 149 over 90.

I told Marcus, "I don't know."

He said, "Give it time."

Week two I was still checking. Numbers were maybe a little lower. Hard to tell. Could have been anything.

Week three, on a Tuesday afternoon, I stood up from my desk in the church office to answer the door for the UPS man and I realized something didn't happen.

The room didn't tilt.

I stood there in the doorway with the package in my hand and I thought about it. I put the package down. I sat back at my desk. I stood up again just to see.

Nothing.

No swim. No hot flash across my forehead. No grabbing the file cabinet.

I sat back down and I put my head in my hands and I cried at my desk with the door open.

Week four the headaches started thinning out. I still got them here and there. But they weren't every day anymore. Some days I'd get to 4 o'clock and realize I hadn't reached for the Tylenol once.

Week five I checked my pressure and it was 138 over 84. I checked it twice because I didn't believe it. I checked it a third time. 136 over 82.

I sat down on the toilet lid in our bathroom holding the cuff. I looked at myself in the mirror.

I said out loud, to nobody, "Oh my God."

Week six I told Dr. Patel. He looked at the numbers on my chart from his own equipment.

He said, "DeShawna. These are the best numbers you've had since I've known you. What are you doing different."

I told him about the amla.

He didn't roll his eyes. Dr. Patel is not that kind of doctor. He just looked at me thoughtful over his glasses and he said, "I don't know anything about that. But I'm not going to tell you to stop. Your numbers are speaking for themselves."

Week eight was the christening.

I woke up at 5:47 AM on October 18th and I laid in bed next to Marcus and I did the thing I always do, which is check in with my body before my feet hit the floor. Any dizziness. Any tightness. Any warning sign.

Nothing.

I got up. I made coffee. I sat on the back porch and watched the sky go from grey to pink to gold over the neighbor's fence.

Marcus came out in his robe and stood behind my chair and put his hands on my shoulders.

He said, "You ready, baby?"

I said, "I'm ready."

The church was full. Every pew. Aunt Regina flew in from Detroit. Kendrick drove down from Birmingham. Jasmine's in-laws came up from Selma. Marcus's whole shift from the construction place came in their Sunday clothes and sat in the back three rows.

Amara was in the little white dress with the lace at the collar. She had a bow in her hair the size of her whole head. She was smiling at everybody. Six months old and already flirting with the congregation.

Pastor Whitfield called Jasmine and Terrell up to the front. Then he called me and Marcus up as the grandparents. I walked up that aisle in my navy blue dress and my sensible shoes and I did not once feel the floor tilt.

Jasmine handed me Amara.

That baby was heavier than I expected. Warm through the little white dress. Her little hand grabbed a fistful of my necklace and would not let go.

Pastor Whitfield said the words. He poured the water over Amara's head. She did not cry, which everybody says is a good sign for the child, though I'm not sure that's in the Bible.

I held my granddaughter over the baptismal font of the church where I have worked for 16 years and where my mother was baptized and where my mother's mother was baptized before her.

I did not go down.

I did not even sway.

Miss Ernestine was in the third row on the right side. When I looked up after the water, her eyes met mine across the sanctuary. She did not smile. She just nodded. One small nod. Nurse to nurse. Woman to woman. That was all.

I am still on two of Dr. Patel's medications. He weaned me off the third one at the four month mark. My last reading was 128 over 79. He is a cautious man and he says we will keep watching.
