bodyText:
Happiness filled me so completely that night, I never thought to question it.
I was lingering beneath the banquet hall's chandeliers, a champagne flute balanced between my fingers, while contentment warmed me from the inside out. Laughter rolled through the crowded room. Glasses chimed together, and passing guests left trails of costly perfume, sharp cologne, and effortless wealth.
This was the future I had chosen, and every part of me wanted it.
Most of all, I loved watching Julian thrive. His tailored suit sharpened the breadth of his shoulders, and confidence made him seem taller as he accepted praise from investors and business partners. He laughed without restraint, perfectly at ease among people eager for his attention.
Rooms like this suited him. He never needed to demand notice; it gathered around him naturally.
Soon, he would belong to me without qualification.
The delay was mine to own. Although we had been together for six years, I still had not revealed what I truly was. I had become the only mother his children remembered, yet he did not know that a wolf lived beneath my skin too.
Whenever I considered confessing, Kira urged patience. One more day, she would insist. One more landmark in our life together, and then we could tell him.
My husband was Julian Miller, the future Alpha of the Silver Moon pack. We had met in college, when I was a gifted chemistry student and he was a businessman searching for an intern at Brightwell Nutrition.
I have always known that claiming my fated mate could never be part of my life. Then Julian appeared: an intelligent, magnetic Alpha who wanted to marry me despite the unremarkable human identity I wore.
It had felt less like chance than a story written for my benefit.
He was raising twins alone. I never learned exactly what had happened to his fated mate, but I believed the moon goddess had offered me another path toward the family I could not stop wanting.
There had been no waiting, no slow construction. Julian and his children had given me a family all at once.
Our home was not flawless. Still, I loved him, and I loved the twins who now felt like my own, more fiercely than I loved anyone else.
The music dropped to a mur. When a spoon rang against crystal, anticipation fluttered through me instead of anxiety. I recognized what was about to happen and moved before Julian had the opportunity, raising my glass as I stepped into view.
"May I steal everyone's attention? Only for a minute."
Conversation dissolved. Faces turned toward me from every corner of the hall.
Surprise crossed Julian's expression before affection replaced it. His smile was warm and faintly indulgent, the one he often gave me when I assumed control of life's smaller moments.
"I won't make a long speech," I said. "There is simply someone here who deserves to know how proud I am of him."
The guests responded with quiet approval. I shifted toward Julian and held his gaze.
"This launch has not come easily. Anyone who has spent time near Julian during the past year has seen what it demanded from him: sleepless nights, endless pressure, and more than a few arguments with his own stubborness."
Julian shook his head while laughter moved through the room.
"But tonight makes one thing clear," I went on. "Vision means something when a person has the determination to defend it. Integrity means something too. And Brightwell Nutrition, the company Julian built, is ready to improve people's lives."
The applause came hard and sincere.
I extended my flute toward him. "For Julian, for Brightwell Nutrition, and for everything still ahead of us."
"Everything ahead," the crowd answered.
Julian bent close enough to brush a familiar kiss across my cheek.
"Thank you," he whispered. "Somehow, you always find the right words."
I trusted that he meant it.
More importantly, I trusted what were together.
His new supplement was already exceeding expectations. Favorable reports were arriving sooner than anyone had predicted, documenting stronger fertility indicators and pregnancies in their earliest stages. The investors could barely contain their excitement, while physicians remained guarded but interested.
Nobody asked who had first conceived the formula.
I did not mind.
Brightwell Nutrition belonged to Julian, so its triumph could belong to him as well. Aplause was never what I needed. My compensation waited at home in the life we shared: the familiar rooms, the dependable rituals, and two children tucked safely into their beds each night.
Across the hall, Emily and Oscar occupied a low table scattered with crayons and coloring books. A pack nanny remained close while they drew. Emily noticed me looking and waved with her entire arm; beside her, Oscar displayed the new gap in his grin.
Love tightened painfully beneath my ribs.
For once, everything seemed stable. I felt protected, as though each difficult compromise I had made had finally proved worthwhile.
At first, the woman's arrival escaped my notice.
One of Julian's partners had cornered me with a discussion about market forecasts, and I was offering polite nods while he spoke. Then the room's rhythm altered. Nothing stopped outright, but laughter faltered and conversations sank into cautious murmurs.
Unease pulled something taut inside me.
I followed the attention toward the doors.
A woman had paused just beyond the entrance. Her fingers were locked together, and she held her shoulders inward as if expecting a blow. The pale blue dress she wore was so plain that the choice seemed calculated. Color had drained from her face, her eyes were inflamed, and the severe line of her mouth suggested that willpower alone was keeping her upright.
I had never seen her before.
My body distrusted her anyway. Kira surged with a warning growl, forcing me to clamp my teeth together before the sound escaped.
A prickle spread over my skin as apprehension twisted low in my abdomen. I tried to dismiss it as response to an uninvited stranger and nothing more.
At my side, Julian had become motionless.
There was no surprise in him and no uncertainty. He looked trapped in ice.
I searched his face. "Julian, what is it?"
Silence was his only answer.
The stranger edged farther into the hall. "I'm sorry," she began, her voice unsteady. "This is a terrible place to do it, and I won't take much of your time."
By then, nobody pretended not to stare. Interest sharpened the guests' expressions, and their attention traveled between the woman and me.
"I needed to tell you how sorry I am," she continued. "For leaving the way I did. For all of it."
Julian's throat worked as he forced down a swallow.
"Camille."
Her name came from him like a wound reopening.
So he knew this woman.
Whatever smile remained on my face disappeared.
"There wasn't another way I could manage," Camille said. "I've practiced this conversation a hundred times, but every version sounded wrong."
Her eyes darted toward me, measuring what she found.
"You deserve an apology too," she added, as though my existence had occurred to her late.
Cold pressure spread behind my breastbone.
I did not understand her regret, nor could I explain why Julian appeared close to breaking apart. I only knew that every instinct me rejected what was unfolding.
Whispers stirred somewhere behind my shoulder. Any ordinary human would have missed them beneath the music, but everyone in this room believed I was ordinary.
They were mistaken.
"It's really her."
"His fated mate."
"She's the twins' birth mother."
For several heartbeats, the phrases carried no meaning. My mind refused to accept them, letting each revelation pass through without taking hold.
Camille's composure began to fracture. "After the twins were born, I left. I was ill, and I couldn't function. Postpartum depression almost killed me."
The floor seemed to roll beneath my feet.
My gaze dropped toward the children's table without conscious thought. Oscar had abandoned his picture. Emily, no longer coloring, watched the adults with confusion pinching her brow.
My pulse battered against my throat.
"I didn't want to desert them," Camille said. "I just wasn't safe then, not for the babies and not for myself."
Postpartum.
That one word refused to move.
"I've been receiving treatment," she said. "I've recovered. I only came because I wanted to see them, even if I get one chance and nothing else."
Julian moved toward her.
His eyes never came to me.
"This conversation can't happen here," he said, keeping his voice low.
Relief softened Camille's features. At the same instant, pain twisted through my stomach with brutal force.
"I understand," she breathed. "I didn't know anywhere else I could find you."
"I'll arrange place for you tonight," Julian told her. "After that, we'll talk."
He spoke with certainty, as if the decision had already been made. My stomach plunged.
Tears escaped freely down her face as she nodded. "Thank you."
Julian turned toward the doors and began leading her out, one hand suspended protectively behind her without quite touching.
I remained where he had left me, still gripping the glass I had raised for him. The words of my own toast mocked me inside the sudden hollow of my head.
Surely, he would glance back.
He never did.
For one reckless moment, I nearly called after him. I wanted to block his path and force every explanation out of him before he took another step.
But an entire ballroom was waiting for my reaction.
Worse, the twins were waiting too.
I fell back on the skill that had carried me through every difficult year.
I adjusted.
When Oscar reached up, I crossed the room and gathered him against my body. Then I bent to press my lips into Emily's hair.
"Everything is fine," I told them softly. "You can finish your pictures."
Around us, the guests lingered in uncomfortable clusters, uncertain whether the celebration had ended.
I drew myself upright, ran a careful palm over my dress, and assembled pleasant expression.
"Please continue enjoying the party," I said. "My husband should be back with us soon."
Gratitude loosened the room. The music swelled again, and interrupted conversations restarted with forced enthusiasm.
Later, people would compliment my dignity. They would call me graceful.
I lifted my champagne once more, and my fingers remained perfectly steady.
"Here's to achievement," I said. "And here's to family."
The response came quieter than before.
I drank while staring at the doorway that had swallowed Julian and Camille. Somewhere beneath my practiced calm, certainty was already taking root: the joy that had filled me when the evening began had vanished for good.
I simply had not discovered its price yet.

Chapter 2: Left Behind
Avery POV
The banquet ended for Julian the instant he followed Camille out.
He never returned.
For a while, I invented excuses on his behalf. Camille had arrived overwhelmed. Julian only needed a few minutes to calm her down. Whatever had pulled him away involved the pack, and once it was handled, he would come back and explain everything.
Still smiling, I watched the door.
Five minutes slipped past. Then ten. By twenty, keeping my expression pleasant had become painful.
Something in my chest fractured with every additional second.
Eventually, the guests abandoned their performance of concern. Talk resumed around me, drifting toward business arrangements, wine, and the food on their plates. Laughter returned with an almost grateful volume. One person praised the dessert while someone else requested the recipe.
Whenever anyone addressed me, I nodded and supplied the expected response. The motions required no thought.
All my attention remained fixed on the doorway.
Then Emily scrubbed at her tired eyes, and Oscar began rocking where he stood. Exhaustion had finally defeated their curiosity. I couldn't leave them surrounded by whispers and artificial smiles any longer.
"I'll take the children upstairs," I told a guest nearby. Politeness held my voice together. "Please stay and enjoy the evening."
Nobody objected. Nobody even made an effort to.
With one child holding each hand, I crossed toward the packhouse's eastern wing and our apartment. Heavy doors swallowed the banquet noise behind us, leaving the corridor unusually quiet and cold.
Oscar dragged his feet like a tiny sleepwalker. His fingers barely curled around mine, and his chin dipped toward his chest every few steps. Emily moved with unnatural precision beside me, gripping my hand hard enough to hurt.
Just before we reached the stairs, her soft voice broke the silence.
"Mommy, who was that lady?"
Pain knotted my stomach.
Emily had always noticed far more than a child her age should. Adults concealed things; she observed the gaps, tucked them away, and waited until she was ready to ask.
She deserved honesty from me.
The problem was that I had no truth to offer.
When she raised her face, Julian's glacial blue eyes stared back at me. She had inherited his focus too, and now she expected me to explain the choices he refused to explain himself.
Without the banquet whispers, I would've known nothing at all. Julian hadn't looked at me before leaving with Camille. He had given me no word, gesture, or warning.
I shaped my mouth into what I hoped passed for reassurance.
"I'm not sure, Sweet Girl," I said. "She might be someone Daddy knew a long time ago."
Even spoken gently, the lie left bitterness on my tongue.
Emily came to a stop and studied me. Her gaze narrowed, searching for whatever I had withheld. Instead of challenging me, she made a quiet, doubtful hum.
Tears would've hurt less than that little sound.
Light spilled beneath our apartment door when we arrived.
I slowed before touching the handle.
There were people talking inside. Then Camille's uneven sobbing rose above the low voices.
I entered and stopped cold.
Beside the couch stood Julian, his body turned toward Camille while one hand moved steadily over her back. I knew that touch. The position of his palm, the measured pressure, the slow rhythm meant to bring someone back from grief. He had soothed me exactly that way whenever I cried.
Camille sat pressed close to him. Damp strands of long blonde hair veiled part of her face, and tears tracked from her reddened brown eyes while her full lips quivered.
Everything about her suggested delicacy.
Too much delicacy to be real.
Julian noticed me and turned his head. That single glance cleaved straight through my heart.
Nothing else about him shifted. His shoulders remained oriented toward Camille, and his hand stayed firmly against her back. His icy gaze skimmed over the children as if they were incidental, then returned to her.
"Camille is staying here," he announced before I could speak. His tone allowed neither debate nor hesitation. "She needs time to settle in."
I expected him to add, "with us."
The words never came.
I also waited for him to acknowledge Emily and Oscar. He failed to do that too.
Oscar sagged sleepily against my thigh. Emily's nails pressed crescents into my palm.
"For how long?" I asked.
Annoyance tightened Julian's face, as though my question itself were unreasonable. "For now."
An answer that explained nothing.
After one small nod, I said, "The kids need baths and bed. They're exhausted."
My voice sounded distant even to me, smooth because I had stripped every feeling out of it.
"Avery..." Julian began.
By then, I had already turned away.
Remaining in that room would've cost me whatever control I still possessed. I needed walls between us, space for my body and my thoughts, anything that might keep the pain from spreading farther.
Steam soon clouded the bathroom while the tub filled. The prospect of warm water briefly revived Oscar, but as soon as I lowered him into it, his eyelids began to droop.
Exactly what I'd expected.
Emily sat rigidly beside him with her knees drawn up. Usually, she filled every room with brightness. Tonight, that light had dimmed, leaving a storm gathered behind her eyes.
Crouching at the tub, I smoothed the wet hair away from her face.
"Hey," I whispered. "You're safe."
No response came.
Kira shifted inside me.
'Let me soothe her,' she offered gently.
I loosened my hold just enough for her presence to surface. A quiet warmth spread from me and softened the air, steady rather than forceful. Some of the tension left Emily's shoulders.
A faint smile touched my lips.
Within minutes, Oscar had fallen completely asleep.
I had just lifted him from the water and wrapped him in a towel when Camille appeared at the bathroom entrance.
From this close, her perfection felt calculated. The ends of her blonde hair were wet and stuck to her shoulders. Crying had left her eyes swollen and her lips puffy. She glanced at Emily, then quickly focused on me.
"Could you use some help?" she asked while dabbing at her eyes.
Her sweetness sounded measured, each word carefully selected.
Before I could refuse, Emily jerked her head from side to side.
"No."
Camille's smile pinched at the corners. "I can lift you out," she said, moving toward the tub without permission.
Fear sharpened Emily's second refusal. "No!"
Her reaction made perfect sense.
Until this evening, Camille had never existed in my daughter's life. She was a stranger who had entered our home without warning, and no one had bothered to tell Emily why.
I placed Oscar on the padded bench and carefully dressed him in his pajamas.
"I can manage," I told Camille, keeping each word civil and restrained. "There's nothing you need to do."
Her mouth flattened into a narrow, cutting curve.
Then, ignoring me, she reached into the tub.
Both hands clamped around Emily's shoulders. The grip was forceful, demanding.
Emily recoiled.
"Stop! Let me go!" Panic shook her voice.
I spun toward them. "Take your hands off my daughter."
The command escaped before caution could soften it.
But Emily was mine.
I had fed her and rocked her through nightmares. Every illness, every burst of laughter, and every tear had found me beside her. I had never failed to come when she needed someone.
A choked noise came from Camille.
"She isn't your daughter," she hissed.
The wounded mask vanished. Cold possession replaced it, stark and vicious in her eyes.
"Yes, I am!" Emily shrieked.
Terror gave her enough strength to wrench herself loose. Her wet body twisted, her foot lost its purchase, and she fell.
Her skull hit the tub's edge with a hard, nauseating crack.
Red immediately streaked her skin.
Oscar jolted awake and screamed.
Crying out, Emily covered the wound with both hands. Blood pushed between her small fingers.
For one impossible beat, my heart seemed to quit moving.
Julian charged into the bathroom.
At once, Camille let go and threw herself backward. She covered her face as sobs overtook her. "She attacked me," she wailed.
Julian's gaze never went to Emily.
His daughter was bleeding from the temple, yet he didn't kneel, inspect the injury, or even ask if she was all right.
Instead, he faced me.
"What have you done?" The accusation in his voice cut sharper than the question.
What the fuck was happening?
"Camille grabbed her," I said. Already on my knees, I pressed a towel against Emily's head. My hands had begun to tremble. "She frightened Emily, and then she slipped."
"You're lying," Julian snapped.
Through her sobs, Emily fought to speak. "Daddy, she grabbed..."
"That's enough," he said, silencing her.
Not even then did he look at his child.
His expression turned glacial. "You're a liar. Avery has taught you to be one."
The words landed harder than any open-handed blow.
Whatever remained intact inside me finally gave way.
I offered no defense. I didn't shout or demand that he see what was in front of him.
My attention narrowed to Emily beneath my hands, Oscar clutching my leg, and the widening stain soaking through the towel.
So I gathered both children close and said nothing.
One person in that room had to keep them safe.
Julian had made it brutally clear that person would never be him.

My kitchen.
The life I had built.

Only there.

Kira shrank back in disgust.
I hadn't found my voice when Camille faced us.
Her attention fixed immediately on Julian's mouth, then shifted to the place on my cheek he'd kissed.
Her expression crumpled.
Nothing about it was restrained or spontaneous. Her shoulders collapsed, her lips quivered, and moisture appeared in her eyes with the precision of a rehearsed performance.

Turning away, she squeezed the mug as if it were the only thing keeping her upright.
In one practiced instant, she became the center of the room.
Julian went to her before he seemed aware he'd moved. He eased the mug from her grip, placed it on the counter, and reached for a second cup that had already been prepared.
That one was for him.
"I remembered how you take it," she murmured.
He accepted the drink.
His eyes never came back to me.
Heat knotted beneath my ribs, vicious and immediate. It hadn't become heartbreak yet.
It was rage.
Clean, bright, cutting rage.

Julian flinched as though my voice had reminded him I was still present.

It wasn't the truth, or it wasn't all of it.
Camille delicately cleared her throat. "I can go upstairs. I don't want to be in the way."

You're fine.
Those two words seemed to fill the kitchen.
Camille compressed her lips, performing another attempt at restraint. Perhaps she was suppressing a smile. Perhaps it was triumph. Bitch.
At last, Julian turned and gave me his full attention.
He rubbed his neck. "Avery, I've been thinking. We need to explain this to the kids."
I said nothing.
"They should understand who Camille is," he went on.
My heartbeat lurched. Of course the twins deserved an explanation about who the fuck this stranger was. But I deserved one too, didn't I? He still hadn't shown enough decency to sit with me and explain any part of this disaster. He had hardly spoken to me at all.

His eyes blinked once.
Only then did comprehension reach him.

Trying to do what?
Make me disappear?

A lot for him, apparently.
Nothing for me.
"I'm overwhelmed," he added softly, offering the admission as if it answered everything.
Then, before I could respond, more words poured out of him. He always kept talking when pressure closed in.
"Maybe we should get the twins out of the house today. They could use some air, and we could do something ordinary. Maybe have a picnic."
A picnic.
"We?"
Surely, he didn't mean what I feared. We had to mean Julian and me. He couldn't intend to take our children, without warning, on an outing with the woman who had abandoned them. He wouldn't shut me out of it. Would he?
His pause answered before he did.
"Camille and me," he said. "It might be easier if you stay home. They need some time to bond with their mother."
The sentence struck harder than an open hand.
I could only stare.
"I'm their mother."
"Yes." Relief briefly lit his face, as if I had finally understood his reasoning. "Of course you are, honey. But they also have to meet their other mom."
Mom.
Fire spread through my chest, and this wasn't some figure of speech. Every breath physically hurt.
I gave him time to hear himself, retract the words, or find some way to include me.
He did none of those things.
Kira's snarl rang through my skull.
I forced down the pressure in my throat before answering.
"I'm not feeling well, so it doesn't matter. Enjoy yourselves."
A crease formed between his eyebrows. "You're sure you aren't angry?"
"Yes."
Angry was far too small a word for what had started consuming me.
I headed for the door. Air wasn't enough. I wanted to cross into rogue territory, tear away my clothes, and surrender control to Kira.
With my hand on the doorway, I spoke without turning. "Oscar is allergic to nuts, including trace amounts. And Emily can't have dairy first thing in the morning."
Camille nodded eagerly. "I know. Of course I do."

Winter air scorched my lungs. I drove myself forward without choosing a destination, caring only about putting more ground between me and that house.
By the time I passed the tree line, Kira was completely awake.
She wasn't frantic anymore, and she wasn't raging. Her presence had become something dense and steady within my bones.
I couldn't have said how long we ran.
We kept moving until strain replaced the ache in my muscles. Kira took control and ripped through the brush, hunting with no restraint. Rabbit after rabbit fell to her. There were more than I could count, far beyond hunger or need.
When I finally returned to my human body, emotion had been scraped out of me. The anger was gone. So were the jealousy and the keen edge of hatred.
Only a hollow space remained.
My fingers had gone numb as I dressed. The journey home took longer, each step weighed down by heavy legs. Worse than the earlier fury was the unnatural stillness inside my head.
When I returned, no one was there.
The silence felt absolute.
The twins weren't laughing or bickering over some meaningless offense. No voices traveled from another room. Stale, undisturbed air filled the house.
Julian had actually taken my children to have a picnic with that woman, leaving me behind.
I stopped in the entryway with my keys clenched in one hand and stared at a point that didn't exist.
My phone began to ring.
At first, I didn't check the display.
There was no need.
After years spent at the edge of pack life, never truly part of it, I knew that number by heart. It belonged to the pack's hospital.
The emptiness inside me tightened into dread.
I answered the call.
"Avery?" The woman on the line maintained a professional tone, but urgency strained every word. "I'm calling from Silver Moon Medical. You need to come here immediately."
Feeling crashed back into me all at once.
"What happened?"
Her silence lasted a fraction too long.
"It's Oscar. He's having a severe allergic reaction. We've stabilized him for the moment, but..."
Whatever followed never reached me.
My hand had already started trembling. I snatched up my keys again while my heart battered my ribs.
"How did this happen?" Even to my own ears, my voice came from somewhere far away.
"We're still determining that," she said with measured caution. "But he ingested something he shouldn't have."

Then he met Camille's eyes.

"No," he agreed. "Fate doesn't."
No. Apparently it didn't.

Julian jerked his head up. "Emily-"
"I don't want Camille in this house," she said, raising her voice over him. Though each word trembled, she held her ground. "She frightens me."
Oscar stirred against my shoulder and weakly raised his head. Confusion creased his forehead before sadness overtook it.
"She scares me too," he whispered.
Everyone went still.
Adelaide started to respond, but no sound emerged. Her mouth closed again. She plainly had not expected either child to reject Camille.
Shock crossed Julian's face, followed by embarrassment. He looked trapped.
Camille rocked on her feet and brought one hand to her chest.
"Everything is spinning," she murmured. "I think... I think I have to sit down."

bodyText:
The music at the Full Moon feast was deafening. I bent down, fumbling with the strap on my heel.
When I looked up, they were already gone. My fated mate, Callum—the feared Alpha of the Red Maple pack—and Freya, my once-best friend.
I started to follow. To lift my dress and run. But the space by his side—my space, the Luna's space—was already gone.
Their bodies were pressed close. Whispering about pack politics. Things I'd never understand.
It was like I wasn't even there. An outsider.
I always knew we'd have an arranged marriage. Callum and me. Finding out we were Mates was no surprise. Our wolves were made for each other. A fatal attraction.
Until Freya proved herself as a lethal fighter.
She used to be the one I told everything to. Now, she was Alpha Callum's sharpest claw. His most trusted Beta.
To everyone in the Alliance, they were the Red Maple pack's power couple.
They shared the glory, the blood, the battles against rogues.
And me? I spent every waking hour in the pack hospital, healing our people, pulling them back from death's door. But to him, I was just a fragile healer who needed protecting.
Forever locked out of his world of blood and instinct.
Callum loved to run his thumb over the back of my neck, right over the spot he'd only partially marked. The possessive scent made my knees weak.
"My sweet Tessa," he'd growl. "You don't need to see the ugliness. Your innocence is what I love."
Then he'd turn. And he and Freya would disappear into the smoke and darkness to handle the pack's violent "business."
This time, watching them walk away, a bone-deep exhaustion washed over me.
I was done. Done chasing a man who would never turn around.
Chapter 1
"Sorry, I need to cancel my reservation for tonight."
I spoke softly into the phone, ending the call from the Alliance's top restaurant.
It was almost eleven.
I'd left the noise of the feast early. Came back alone to the empty Pack House.
My phone lit up again. Sarah, from the Alliance Medical Center.
"Tessa! Spill it!" Her voice was buzzing with excitement. "Was it romantic? Did Alpha Callum book out the whole place for you? You just healed your hundredth critical patient! Did he give you the Luna's moonstone? Are you two finally going to complete the bond?!"
Every question was a fresh stab of pain. My wolf whimpered.
I swallowed the bitterness in my throat and stared at my reflection in the mirror. Alone.
"No," I cut her off, my voice flat. "He had to leave. Something came up."
I hung up before she could reply.
I stripped off the designer gown I'd bought just for tonight. Slipped into a silk nightdress and sat by the floor-to-ceiling window.
Fate was a joke.
My pack, Silver Moon, was part of the Northern Alliance. We're known for healing. And for our power on the Council.
On this continent, a place of shadows and secrets, Red Maple needed us. They needed our votes and our medical resources to get Callum elected as the Alliance Chairman. And we needed their strength, their warriors, to keep our family's power in the North.
We were fated Mates. A perfect political union. Our souls were meant to be one.
But in this house, I could count on one hand the number of nights we spent truly alone together.
Tonight was supposed to be different.
It was the full moon. Callum was finally on leave. I thought… I hoped… he'd finally see me. See my worth.
But just as the feast was ending, Freya burst in. Dressed in black combat gear.
She spread a map of the northern border on the table.
Two hours. They sat shoulder-to-shoulder. Whispering in the low growl of wolf-speak.
I couldn't get a single word in.
I was just a decoration. A ghost. Watching the clock tick past our reservation. Watching them exist in a world that wasn't mine.
It was three in the morning when he finally came back.
The smell of blood and cold night air hit me as the bedroom door opened.
The second his eyes met mine, the Mate bond devoured him.
He crossed the room in three long strides. His large hand locked around my wrist like a vice.
"Callum, you—"
He pulled me against his hard chest.
Then his head dipped, and he kissed me like a savage. Desperate. Draining the calming scent from my skin like a dying addict.
My mind screamed. Push him away.
He had no right. No right to ignore me, then come back and take from me like this.
But the bond is a killer.
My legs gave out. I could only cling to his shoulders as he pushed me back onto the massive bed.
…
An hour later.
The sound of the shower stopped.
The breathless, soul-crushing passion on the bed felt like a dream. A hallucination.
Callum walked out, a towel slung low on his hips.
The fire in his eyes was gone. Replaced by the cold indifference of an Alpha.
"Why did you leave the feast early tonight?" he asked, his voice casual as he towel-dried his hair.
I clutched the sheets to my chest. My body ached from his roughness.
"You were busy with your map," I said, meeting his gaze. "The restaurant closed hours ago."
Callum stopped.
His brows drew together. The air in the room grew thin with the force of his Alpha power.
"Tessa, when will you grow up?"
He grabbed a clean shirt and pulled it on.
"Freya got hurt on the front lines tonight! As my Beta, she risks her life for this territory! The least you could do is be on standby in the pack hospital, not sit here throwing a fit."
Every word was a defense of her.
Throwing a fit.
I'd been on my feet for over ten hours, pulling his dying pack members back from the brink.
In his eyes, that was throwing a fit.
Tears burned my eyes. I bit my lip so hard I tasted blood.
I couldn't cry.
"You're right. It's my fault," I heard myself say. My voice was numb. Empty.
I dropped my gaze, refusing to look at him.
Callum's jaw relaxed.
He was satisfied with my surrender. He thought he'd fixed it.
He walked over. That same hand that had just claimed me now patted my head like I was a pet.
"Stop sulking. Get some sleep." His tone was a condescending gift. "Freya's waiting in the study. We need to debrief."
The door clicked shut.
The room was silent again.
I turned my head. Through the crack under the door, I could see the warm yellow glow from the study across the hall.
My phone buzzed, shattering the suffocating quiet.
The screen flashed: FATHER.
He was a high elder on the Alliance Council. The leader of the Silver Moon pack.
I took a deep breath and answered.
"Tessa." My father's stern voice came through. "The Alliance roster is being updated. When is Callum going to hold the official Luna marking ceremony for you? Our family's alliance cannot falter."
I stared at the sliver of light from the study door.
This must be what it felt like to be completely numb. I couldn't even feel the pain anymore.
I swallowed all the despair in my throat. My voice was surprisingly calm.
"Dad, Callum is busy with the territory expansion and his campaign for Chairman. He doesn't have time for a ceremony."
Chapter 2
"Tessa, the election for Alliance Chairman is next month."
The faces of the Silver Moon elders were grim on the secure video call.
"The packs are tearing each other apart behind the scenes. Callum has the most support right now. For the good of our family, for our power on the High Council, you must have him complete the Luna marking. Solidify this union now."
I stared at the screen.
In their eyes, I was just a pawn. A piece to hold their power in place.
I took a sip of cold water, my throat raw.
"I'm sorry to disappoint you all." I looked right at them, my voice flat.
The elders' faces tightened.
"I'm breaking the engagement," I said, each word sharp and clear. "And I'm going to reject the bond."
The call exploded.
They were yelling. Pounding on tables. Calling me insane. Accusing me of risking everything, of throwing away our entire family's work against the vampires.
I couldn't be bothered to listen. I cut the feed.
Finally. Silence.
The next day, at the medical center. Noon.
I was packing my life's work into cardboard boxes. Years of research. Formulas for my advanced healing serums.
Freya pushed the door open. She held two cups of hot coffee.
She wasn't wearing her usual aggressive combat gear. Today, it was a soft, cream-colored sweater.
It made her look like she used to. The gentle, kind friend I once knew.
"Tessa, what are you doing?" She stared at the boxes, shocked. She walked over and offered me a coffee.
Her brow was furrowed with concern. Her voice dripped with fake sympathy.
"Did you and Callum fight again? He was so distracted on the border last night. I thought you two had made up."
I didn't take the coffee.
My eyes were glued to her neck.
As she moved, a gleaming moonstone necklace slipped out from her sweater.
The Luna's heirloom. A sacred artifact of protection.
It was only supposed to be given by an Alpha to his Mate during the sacred marking ceremony.
My stomach lurched. A wave of nausea hit me hard.
"Oh, this…"
Freya followed my gaze and clutched at her collar.
She blushed, but her eyes were wide with innocence. "Please don't be mad at Callum. The border was dangerous last night. The dark energy from the bloodsuckers… it was messing with my head. Callum insisted I wear it. He said it would soothe my wolf."
She reached out and took my hand, her voice conspiratorial, like we were still best friends.
"He even made a bet with me. He said, 'My fragile little Tessa will probably cry when she sees this.' See? He loves teasing us."
He used my pain as a joke.
He used the Goddess's blessing to protect another woman.
"Really." I pulled my hand away. My voice was ice. "You two are so in sync."
"Tessa, don't be like this. We're just comrades-in-arms…" Freya's eyes welled up. She looked so hurt. So wronged.
Familiar footsteps echoed in the hall.
Callum's tall frame filled the doorway.
He glanced at the boxes on the floor, a lazy smirk on his face.
"Looks like I won," he said to Freya, his tone full of arrogant indulgence. "The car's outside. Go wait for me."
Freya nodded obediently. As she passed me, a flicker of triumph flashed in her downcast eyes.
The door closed. We were alone.
Callum strode toward me.
He was so sure of himself.
He thought I was just throwing a tantrum. He thought I could never leave him.
"How long are you going to keep this up?"
His Alpha presence pressed in on me. He reached for the back of my neck, a habit.
I turned my head, dodging his touch.
Callum's hand froze in midair.
His eyes darkened. Annoyance flashed across his face.
"I'm not throwing a fit," I said, meeting his gaze without flinching. "I just informed the Silver Moon Council. This union is over."
Callum stared for a second, then let out a short, sharp laugh.
"Tessa, stop playing these childish games. Your family needs me as Chairman more than anyone. They'd never agree."
He stepped closer, his voice laced with arrogant certainty.
"So I lent Freya the necklace. Is that it? You don't understand the fighting on the front lines. It was a tool to keep her alive. You're perfectly safe here. You don't need it."
"It's not just the union."
I took a deep breath. I closed my eyes.
"I'm rejecting you."
"Are you insane?!"
Panic flashed in his eyes. He grabbed my shoulders, his grip like steel.
For the first time, those ambitious, arrogant eyes showed real fear. The fear of his mate, his prize, slipping from his grasp.
"Don't you dare use this to get my attention!" he snarled, his voice a low growl of fury and shock.
"I'm not trying to get your attention!"
I shoved him with all my strength. A bitter, mocking smile twisted my lips.
"Callum, do you think being a Luna is just wearing a necklace and looking pretty? You think Freya's blood is the only sacrifice that matters?"
I pointed at the boxes of top-secret serums behind me.
"It was ME! My talent, my work, that patched up every hole you tore in this pack! Without me, your precious warriors would all be dead!"
Callum just stood there. Stunned.
He'd never seen me like this. Never seen me so sharp. So broken.
He reached for me, an instinct. But the ice in my eyes stopped him cold.
"I am done being second best to Freya. I am done with you taking and taking and taking."
I grabbed the heaviest box from the table and slammed it into his chest as I pushed past him.
"You and Freya are so perfect for each other. From now on, she can be the one to fix all your problems."
The second I stepped out of the medical center, the cold northern wind hit my face.
The pain of a soul being torn apart was still there.
But I could finally breathe.
A mountain had been lifted off my chest.
Chapter 3
The next day, the door to my office flew open.
"Tessa!" Sarah was pale, her voice shaking. "The border patrol was ambushed by high-level rogues. Freya's left arm… it was completely torn off!"
Even after everything, the healer in me took over. I sprinted toward the ICU.
But I barely made it into the hallway. I hadn't even pulled on my gloves when a wave of furious Alpha energy slammed into me.
Callum was there. Covered in blood.
His eyes were crimson. A beast on the verge of snapping.
He didn't ask for my help. He grabbed my shoulders and slammed me against the cold wall.
"Are you satisfied now?!" he roared, the stench of blood washing over me.
Pain shot through my back. I winced. "Let go. I have to stop the bleeding…"
"Drop the fake concern, Tessa!"
Callum's power crushed down on me. His eyes were full of cold hatred and raw panic.
"If you hadn't thrown your little tantrum yesterday, if you hadn't threatened to break our bond and sent a shockwave through the pack's mind-link, Freya never would have been distracted! She never would have gotten hurt!"
I froze.
The sheer insanity of his accusation shattered the last bit of respect I had for him.
"You're blaming a tactical failure on me?" I was trembling with rage.
"Tactical failure? What do you know about war?" He leaned in, his voice dripping with scorn. "If we weren't out there bleeding for you, fighting off our enemies, those little formulas you brew in your perfect, sterile lab would be worthless! Did you have to do this? Did you have to prove your point in the cruelest way possible?"
The pressure of his soul-bond, combined with the aftershocks of my rejection, sent waves of pain through my heart.
Tears spilled from my eyes, hot and uncontrollable.
Seeing me cry, Callum thought he'd won. He thought I finally understood my "mistake."
The beast in him retreated slightly.
He let go of my shoulders and raised a hand, a disgusting, fake tenderness in his gesture, as he tried to wipe my tears away.
"Grow up. Stop throwing fits over the pack's security," he commanded, his voice full of the arrogance of a king, sure that I would bow my head like always.
"Don't touch me."
I jerked my head away, disgusted. I scrambled back, putting space between us.
Callum's hand hung in the air. His face turned to stone.
"Understood, Alpha." I met his eyes, my voice dead.
His pupils contracted. The word clearly stung him.
"From this moment on, I am no longer your personal healer." I ripped the stethoscope from my neck. "Since my serums are so worthless, you can figure it out yourselves."
"Callum…"
A weak voice came from the hospital room.
Freya was propped up in bed, her face pale. She tugged pathetically at Callum's bloodstained sleeve.
"Don't fight with Tessa… She just cares about you too much. I don't blame her for losing her temper and distracting me… cough, cough…"
What a perfect, noble little victim.
Looking at this pair of arrogant, self-righteous pricks, I let out a sharp, mocking laugh.
I walked over to the medical waste bin and threw my white coat—the symbol of the pack's chief healer—inside.
Then I turned and walked away.
…
For the next two weeks, Callum gave me the silent treatment.
He thought he could break me. Force me to come crawling back.
He even spent a fortune hiring a specialist from another territory to heal Freya, just to prove he didn't need me.
I didn't care. I just kept packing my things, getting ready to leave Red Maple for good.
Two weeks later, in the afternoon.
I had just left the main administration building when a healed Freya blocked my path.
She wore a new, expensive trench coat. Her left arm was perfectly fine. Her face held the gracious smile of a victor.
"Tessa, you've been sulking for two weeks. Isn't it time to let it go?"
She walked toward me, her gaze condescending.
"Go apologize to Callum. He'll forgive you. After all, even I've decided to forgive you for your little outburst."
"Forgive me?"
I stared into her eyes, almost laughing.
"Freya, you've never even read a basic tactics manual, have you?"
The smile on her face froze. "What are you talking about?"
"I'm talking about how you rush into every ambush with nothing but brute force. The only reason you're so reckless is because you knew I was always there to patch you up."
I stepped toward her. My voice was quiet, but every word was a blade.
"You're a parasite. You've been feeding off my medical resources, using my advanced serums to build your 'greatest warrior' reputation. Without me, the vampires would have killed you a hundred times over."
"You—!" Freya's mask of grace shattered. Her face went white.
I ignored her.
Looking at this face that was once so familiar, all I felt was a cold, alien distance.
Chapter 4
"Move." I shoved past Freya's shoulder, not giving her a second glance.
I'd only taken a few steps when my phone started vibrating like crazy.
It was the Red Maple head of security.
"Miss Tessa! Something terrible has happened!" His voice was choked with panic. "The High Council just issued a top-level warrant! The formula for the secret healing serum… the one your father sponsored in the council… it's been stolen by the vampires! The Tribunal is launching a full investigation!"
I stopped dead. The blood drained from my face.
"That's impossible!" I choked out. "The highest level of access to that data is restricted to me, Callum, and the frontline commander, Freya! The system is physically isolated!"
Only ragged breathing came from the other end of the line.
Ten minutes later. The emergency council room.
The air was thick with tension.
Callum sat at the head of the table, his face a thundercloud.
Freya was at his right, her hands clenched so tight her knuckles were white.
"Run a full diagnostic on the internal network. Cross-reference the access logs for all three of our terminals, now." I braced my hands on the table, breaking the silence. "The formula couldn't have just vanished. There has to be a trace."
"Enough."
Callum's voice was cold. Merciless.
He looked up at me, his eyes empty of any warmth. He was looking at an enemy.
"There's no need to check." He announced it to the whole room. "The secure tablet was lost on the front lines, yes. But the vampires couldn't have cracked it without a high-level override code. Your father's political rivals have already submitted 'evidence' to the Tribunal. They're claiming he abused his authority as a sponsor to leak the code to the vampires."
My eyes widened in disbelief.
"Callum, you know that's a lie! What are you talking about?!"
"To protect the Red Maple pack, and to secure the front line, I will be writing to the Tribunal to support their claim. I will confirm that your father's negligence led to the leak. It's the most logical way to limit the damage."
The room gasped.
He was going to send my father to his execution.
The meeting ended in a stunned silence.
In the empty hallway, I blocked Callum's path.
"You and Freya lost the secure tablet on patrol last week! You were ambushed by vampires!" My voice was a raw scream, my eyes burning. "It was YOUR mistake! Why are you letting them pin this on my father?! Why are you sacrificing him to cover for Freya?!"
Callum's huge frame loomed over me.
There was no guilt in his eyes. Only the cold fury of an Alpha who had been questioned in public.
"When did you become so vicious, Tessa?" He looked down at me, his voice freezing cold. "Freya is the core of Red Maple's fighting force. If I admit the mistake was made on the front lines, she'll be executed for treason by the Tribunal. The entire northern defense will collapse!"
He grabbed my chin, his voice full of righteous certainty.
"Letting your father, a man caught in a political storm anyway, take the fall for 'negligent oversight' is the most rational decision for an Alpha. It keeps our sharpest weapon safe. Once he's served some time, once I've beaten back the vampires and become Chairman, I'll use my authority to get him out."
"Rational?" I laughed, a broken, hysterical sound. Tears splashed onto his hand. "That's my FATHER! The man you swore to honor and respect! Who the hell do you think you are, to assume you can control everything?!"
Callum shoved my hand away and adjusted his tie, irritated.
"For the good of the pack, some sacrifices are necessary. You need to learn to see the bigger picture, instead of acting like a hysterical child."
He left me there. He and Freya walked away without a backward glance.
I watched them go, my chest heaving.
Was my heart breaking?
No. There was nothing left to break.
This was the man I had loved for more than a decade.
To protect his obedient little soldier, because he arrogantly decided a politician's life was worth less than a warrior's, he had thrown my father away like garbage.
The next day.
The news was everywhere.
SILVER MOON ELDER ACCUSED OF TREASON! SECRET SERUM LEAKED TO VAMPIRES!
I watched the report on the television. I felt nothing. Just a vast, empty wasteland inside me.
Three in the afternoon.
I took off the uniform with the Red Maple crest.
I turned on the shredder. One by one, I destroyed all of it. My private notes. My unpublished formulas.
If my work was worthless to him, then it could disappear forever.
I walked into the main hall of the Pack House, carrying the last box.
Callum was on the sofa, reading a battle report. He frowned when he saw the box.
He stood up and walked over to me.
No apology. No guilt.
He even tried to put his arm around my waist.
I shifted my body, just enough to avoid his touch.
Callum's hand fell to his side. He made a small, irritated sound.
"Still sulking?" He looked down at me, his voice dripping with arrogant pity. "I've already handled the Council. I promise, your father won't be executed. After he serves his time, I'll use Red Maple's resources to get him a quiet, comfortable position. Happy now?"
In his mind, this was a massive favor.
He was sure I had nowhere else to go. Sure that his little hothouse flower couldn't survive without him.
"There's a high-level dinner tonight. For morale." He glanced at his watch, his tone a command. "You'll wait for me at home. And don't cause any more trouble."
I looked at this cold, blindly confident Alpha. And I smiled.
"Okay," I said softly. My voice was impossibly calm.
A satisfied smirk touched Callum's lips. He turned and walked up the stairs.
I looked away, clutched my box, and pushed open the heavy main doors of the Pack House.
The northern sun was setting, staining the sky the color of blood. A dry, cold wind blew away the last trace of my scent from the home I was leaving behind.
I walked out of the prison I had lived in for over a decade.
And I never looked back.
He had no idea I was never coming back.
Chapter 5
An hour later, I stood in front of my parents' estate in the heart of Silver Moon territory, suitcase in hand.
The moment I pushed the door open, I froze.
My father was sitting in a plush armchair in the study, wearing a silk robe, calmly reading an old book.
A fire crackled in the hearth.
This was not a man about to be tried for treason.
"Dad?" I asked, my voice cautious. "The news said…"
"The news," my father scoffed, closing the book. He looked at me, his eyes sharp. "Tessa, did you think I'd spent thirty years on the Council just to be some pushover?"
He pulled a file from a hidden compartment and tossed it on the table in front of me.
The seal of the High Werewolf Council was stamped on top, blood-red and stark.
"Application for political protection and countersuit," my father said, his voice cold, almost cruel. "It was approved three days ago. The Tribunal has already secretly acquired the true communication logs from the Red Maple front line."
My head snapped up. "You knew?"
"I saw Callum's pathetic little plan before he even made his move," my father said, standing up. He looked down at the file, his voice full of scorn. "He thought he could throw an elder under the bus to cover up his and Freya's mess? I cut off Red Maple's medical funding and revoked Silver Moon's political protection for them on the Council the moment I got the file."
My heart stopped.
"Without Silver Moon's legal cover," my father sneered, "Callum's violent expansion, his forced absorption of rogue packs… all of it is a death sentence in the eyes of the Council. He thought he was saving his precious front line. In reality, he just signed his own execution warrant."
At dinner, my mother pushed a plane ticket across the table to me.
"Sunpeak," she said softly. "It's in the southern neutral zone. The weather is beautiful. No one knows you there. Go open your own medical center, Tessa. This time, live for yourself. The Silver Moon pack will always have your back."
I looked at the ticket, my eyes burning.
That night, as I was packing, my phone vibrated nonstop.
Callum: Where are you? Come back. Now.
Callum: You think you can hide? I'm your Alpha. I can track your mate-scent.
Callum: Don't make me come get you, Tessa.
I stared at the screen, my fingers cold.
Not a single word of concern. Just commands. And the rage of a king who had been defied.
Suddenly, I heard a commotion downstairs.
My door was pushed open.
Freya walked in carrying an expensive bottle of wine as a peace offering, two grim-faced Silver Moon guards behind her.
She had somehow used Red Maple's last shred of diplomatic privilege to force her way into the estate.
Her eyes were red and swollen. She was trying to put on her old, pathetic act.
"Tessa, I know you're angry," she said, her voice trembling. "But Callum said it was your father who took the blame voluntarily. He didn't force anyone. Please, come back with me. His feral side is getting out of control…"
"Voluntarily?"
I shot up from my seat and slapped the bottle out of her hand. It shattered onto the carpet, spilling dark red wine.
Freya flinched back.
"You have the nerve to say that?" I stared at her, my voice like ice. "Without my family's medical backing, without Silver Moon's political shield, your Red Maple warriors are nothing but walking corpses to the vampires."
"Tessa, you—"
"You think you're the sharpest claw?" I stalked toward her. "You're just a reckless fool who only survived this long because I was there to clean up your messes. Now, the person who cleaned up your messes is gone."
Freya's face went white. Her lips trembled, unable to form words.
A surge of Luna power exploded from me. The pressure slammed into her, making her stumble backward.
"Get out."
She scrambled out of the room like a beaten dog.
I slammed the door shut and leaned against it, panting.
From my drawer, I took out a small packet of herbs—the kind used to numb the physical backlash of sensory connections. I stirred it into a glass of water and drank it down.
Then, I closed my eyes. I pricked my finger, drawing a single drop of blood. And I whispered the ancient words.
"I, Tessa of the Silver Moon pack, reject you, Callum of the Red Maple pack, as my mate and my Alpha."
A searing pain shot through me as the thin, spiritual tether of our bond snapped.
Then, silence.
I picked up my phone, found Callum's number, and held down the block button.
Outside, the moonlight fell on the plane ticket to Sunpeak.
Tomorrow, the southern sun would be mine alone.

Ophelia's husband Harold died on their fiftieth anniversary.

At his graveside, her granddaughter blamed the planets.

"It was written in the stars, Grandma. Mercury was in retrograde."

Harold died that morning holding Ophelia's hand, and the anniversary party became a funeral.

The cake went into the freezer untouched.

Now her granddaughter, who read horoscopes every morning, wanted Ophelia to know it was "the universe's timing," and she was planning to say so at the Thanksgiving table.

If someone gave the stars credit for your husband's life, read this.

Ophelia didn't say a word at the grave.

She held her granddaughter's arm, because Hailey was crying too.

But that night, she sat on Harold's side of the bed for a long time.

She thought about letting it go.

Hailey was nineteen and grieving her grandpa in the only language she had.

But Ophelia remembered her own grandmother's funeral in 1966, when the minister didn't come and the family "kept it simple."

Nobody mentioned God, and nobody mentioned heaven, and Ophelia went home at nine years old believing her grandma had just disappeared.

She didn't want Hailey believing Harold had just disappeared.

So she tried talking to Hailey about heaven, gently, over coffee.

Hailey said, "Grandma, that's a nice story, but the stars don't lie."

So she tried saying nothing and letting Hailey's mother handle it.

Her daughter said, "Mom, let her believe what helps her right now."

That night Ophelia realized she was being asked to let her husband's whole life be explained by a planet.

On Wednesday she told her friend Winnie from the choir, who had sung next to her for thirty-eight years and buried her own husband in 2015.

Winnie listened, and then she smiled.

"Ophelia, that girl isn't wrong about everything. Harold's life was written in the stars."

"She's just got the wrong author."

"Don't fight her. Finish her sentence."

Then Winnie pulled a dark chocolate shirt out of her choir bag.

At the top, in small, spaced cream letters, sat inside a little gold constellation with stars connected by thin lines.

Underneath, in big, bold cream letters, it finished.

"Don't Thank Your Lucky Stars. Thank The One Who Named Them."

Ophelia laughed for the first time since the funeral.

It was exactly what Winnie said: finish the sentence.

Every grandmother grew up saying "thank your lucky stars."

And every church girl knows the Psalm: He counts the number of the stars, and calls them all by their names.

The shirt agreed with Hailey that the stars were there, and then pointed past them.

Ophelia had faith shirts already.

A gray one with "Faith Hope Love" in thin script.

A white blouse with a cross necklace she'd worn to every funeral since 1980.

They were quiet, respectful and invisible.

This one had a beautiful little star pattern Hailey would actually like.

It answered the horoscope talk without a single unkind word.

And it was big enough to read across a Thanksgiving table.

Ophelia almost didn't order it.

"Will Hailey think I'm making fun of her?"

Then she remembered Harold, every summer on the porch, pointing out the Big Dipper to Hailey and saying, "Somebody hung all those just for you, sweet pea."

She ordered hers in dark chocolate, the color of Harold's old work jacket.

She wore it to Thanksgiving.

Hailey read it and stopped in the doorway.

"Grandma."

"I'm finishing your sentence, honey."

At dinner, Hailey kept looking at the shirt.

After pie, she found Ophelia on the back porch, looking up.

"Did Grandpa really believe God named all of them?"

"Every one," Ophelia said.

"He used to say the stars were God showing off."

Hailey laughed and cried at the same time.

Then she asked, "Will you show me the Big Dipper like he used to?"

So Ophelia did, and she told Hailey the Psalm, and Hailey asked her to say it twice.

The shirt kept going after that.

Hailey asked for the Psalm in a text, and she set it as the lock screen on her phone.

At choir practice, two other widows asked Winnie where to get one.

And in December, Hailey came to the Christmas Eve service for the first time in four years and sat right next to her grandmother.

The story of Ophelia isn't about a horoscope.

It's about the women who won't let anyone give the stars credit for what God did.

Every Christian widow knows how quickly the world tries to explain away the life she shared with him.

And every one of them knows the grandkids are listening to see what Grandma says about heaven.

This shirt is not for everybody.

It's not for the woman who reads her horoscope "just for fun" every morning.

It's not for the woman who stays quiet so the grieving young people aren't uncomfortable.

It's for the woman who has buried the love of her life and still believes she'll see him again.

The woman who taught her grandkids to look up.

The woman who knows who named every star.

If that's you, you already know why this line matters.

Here's what happens when you wear it.

A young person reads it and says, "Wait, that's so pretty."

Another widow at church asks you where you got it.

Your grandkids ask you to tell them the stars story again.

And the person who believed in "the universe" starts asking you about God.

bodyText:
A werewolf only has one fated mate in their lifetime. But my Alpha husband Derek refused to acknowledge me.
All because I was human. Six years ago, to be with him, I was forced to sign a humiliating breeding contract with the pack elders.
Bear an heir within one year: receive ten million.
Bear an heir within three years: receive three million.
If no pregnancy occurred within six years, I could not interfere with my husband's affairs outside the marriage.
Derek's eyes burned red as he roared at me: "Did you become my mate because of me, or because of the Thorn Pack's fortune?!"
From that day on, to punish me, he deliberately brought his assistant Camilla to every event, doting on her right in front of me.
Until the sixth year, when he moved Camilla into the villa and put my Luna necklace around her neck in front of everyone.
"Camilla is pure and kind. She deserves this necklace more than you do."
He thought no matter what he did, I would never leave.
But he didn't know there was another clause on the second page of that contract:
If we still hadn't produced a child within six years, either party could choose to terminate the mate bond.
Our contract was set to expire in seven days.
Chapter 1
At the Moonlight Gala, my husband Derek brought his assistant Camilla for the fifth time.
Everyone toasted her, and when she couldn't handle the moonwine, Derek's arm shot out to block the drinks for her. He picked the tenderest venison and placed it on her plate. He even draped his own cloak over her shoulders.
I watched it all. Didn't argue. Didn't make a scene. Didn't say a word. I just quietly got up and left.
Because six years ago, the pack elders had forced me to sign that humiliating contract:
Bear an heir within one year: ten million.
Bear an heir within three years: three million.
If no pregnancy within six years, no interference with my husband's affairs.
And this year was the sixth year.
The entire pack was waiting to see me humiliate myself. They were waiting for me to run up to Camilla with red eyes and start a fight, just like the last four times.
The young wolves had even started a live thread on the Moon Night Forum:
"What's Chloe going to do to Camilla this time?"
The comments were on fire.
"Everyone knows Chloe's just a human who clawed her way to Luna status on a breeding contract. Six years and not even a hint of a pup? She deserved to be replaced."
"Camilla's bloodline is way purer than Chloe's. She should be the pack's Luna."
"Chloe's just a greedy leech. She should crawl back to the human world where she belongs."
"Haha, if Chloe sees this, she's definitely going to throw another tantrum!"
A year ago, those comments would have kept me up all night. I'd have argued with every single one of them, desperately trying to defend my marriage.
Now I felt nothing. I calmly liked the comment supporting Derek and replied:
"You're right."
That move shocked the entire pack.
Even Derek's beta, Ryan, couldn't resist. He started a live stream and tracked Derek down at the gala to ask him directly:
"Derek, even that proud human Chloe has been tamed by you? Tell me your secret."
Derek didn't answer. He was staring at his phone at a new message.
[Alpha, the Luna just entered the pack's private vault.]
Derek let out a cold laugh. Then he sent me the link to Ryan's stream and sneered at the camera:
"Tamed? Please. Only money shuts her up."
"I bet this time it'll take at least ten million to make her happy. Am I right, my Luna?"
Watching my husband mock me like that, my heart ached with a sharp, stabbing pain.
The mate mark over my heart kept burning, reminding me—
A werewolf only has one fated mate. The bond forged under the Moon Goddess is unbreakable.
But in Derek's eyes, I was always just that pathetic human who sold herself for money.
Even after six years. Even with both our marks on each other's skin. He still thought money was all it took to shut me up.
I brushed away the tears I hadn't even realized were there, closed the stream, and walked into the private vault.
Moonstones. Gold bars. Century-old antique jewelry.
Everything was there. One piece could buy a mansion.
I didn't look at any of it. I walked straight to the back, opened the drawer, and took out a yellowed piece of parchment.
The truth was, when I married into the Thorn Pack six years ago, I'd signed two contracts.
The one Derek had seen was only half the story. There was another one—a termination clause.
"If no child is produced within six years, either party may choose whether to continue the bond."
I stared at the words until my vision blurred. Memories flooded back.
At eighteen, I met Derek at a campus ball. He'd spotted me from across the room and immediately recognized me as his fated mate.
He pursued me relentlessly. He wanted to bond with me.
And I fell for him just as hard.
So our first year of marriage was pure bliss.
In spring, he took me to the islands, where we ran barefoot along the shore chasing the ebbing moonlight.
In summer, we escaped to the Moonlight Springs, where he swore under the stars that he'd love me forever.
In autumn, we walked the Maple Avenue, and he clumsily carved our names into the falling leaves.
In winter, he took me to the far northern snowfields, shifted into his wolf form, and carried me across the tundra chasing the northern lights.
We were drowning in happiness. Our cross-species marriage was celebrated throughout the pack.
Until the Moonlight Gala in our third year, when the elders started pressuring me to produce an heir.
And the contract I'd signed with the council found its way to Derek's ears.
His eyes went wild and red as he demanded: "Chloe, did you become my mate because of me, or because of the Thorn Pack's fortune?!"
After that, everything fell apart. No matter how many times I explained that I'd only signed it so I could marry him, he'd already decided I was nothing but a greedy fraud.
From that day on, Derek was a different man.
He stopped using my name. In public, he only called me "Luna."
He promoted Camilla—who'd been just a regular office worker—to his personal assistant.
He deliberately brought her to every gala. He danced with her in front of me. He draped his jacket over her shoulders. He hovered over her like a devoted husband.
The elders said the Alpha treated Camilla more like a wife than he'd ever treated me.
At first, I cried. I screamed. I fell apart.
Derek just watched me break, cold and distant. Then he turned around and showed Camilla even more affection, using it as a knife to carve me open again and again, forcing me to confess to a crime I never committed.
He thought no matter what he did, I would never leave.
But he didn't know there was another clause on the second page of that contract:
If we still hadn't produced a child within six years, either party could choose to terminate the mate bond.
And now the six-year contract was up. Time for this whole farce to end.
I took the contract straight to the town hall and started the final process.
In seven days, the mate bond would be severed.
I would disappear from Derek's world forever.
Chapter 2
When I walked out of the town hall, it was pouring rain.
Derek's call came through. His voice dripped with sarcasm. "Chloe, you've been in the private vault long enough. How much more do you plan to take?"
I was quiet for a moment. My voice came out rough. "What do you want?"
"What do I want?" He let out a cold laugh. "We have important guests coming to the villa tonight. Get your ass back here and prepare the banquet. Since you're taking the Thorn Pack's money, at least do your job as Luna."
Even though I'd already made up my mind to leave, his open contempt still cut deep.
It took me a moment to swallow the bitterness. "Fine."
But my obedience didn't satisfy him. If anything, it made him angrier.
"Of course. As long as there's money involved, you'll do anything, won't you?"
"Let's see how long you can keep up this little act."
He hung up.
By the time I got home, I was soaked to the bone.
There were guests coming tonight. I didn't want any drama. I just wanted to get through this banquet quietly and leave.
But when I pressed my fingerprint to the smart lock, an error flashed.
[Unauthorized entry.]
I froze. It took me a moment to understand.
They'd revoked my access.
I let out a bitter laugh, then knocked on the door. No answer.
I rang the bell a dozen more times. Still nothing.
In that downpour, wearing nothing but a thin soaked dress, I huddled in the corner by the door for two full hours.
Finally, the villa door swung open.
The butler stepped out, his face cold as stone as he looked down at me.
"Luna, you may enter. The Alpha said that since you're taking the pack's money, you should follow the pack's rules. Two hours is just a small punishment. He hopes you'll behave yourself in the future."
I was shivering, pale as death, but I understood.
Derek had made me stand in the rain on purpose.
I let out a hollow, bitter laugh and stumbled inside.
Dizzy and sick, I somehow managed to get everything ready for the banquet.
That night, the villa blazed with light and laughter.
Camilla stood at the top of the stairs in a silver gown I'd never seen before. And around her neck hung my Luna necklace.
She walked toward me with a wine glass, her voice soft and sweet where everyone could hear.
"Luna, I hope you don't mind. I asked Derek if I could borrow this necklace to try on."
My head was spinning. I didn't answer her. I just turned to leave.
Then she grabbed my wrist.
"Luna, you really can't forgive me, can you?"
Her voice suddenly shot up. "Ah! Luna, why are you pushing me—"
Before she even finished, she was falling backward, tumbling down the stairs.
"Camilla!"
A blur of motion. Derek caught her, pulling her close to his chest.
The whole hall gasped.
Camilla trembled in his arms, her voice shaking with fear. "Derek, I know Luna didn't mean to. She just doesn't like me. I don't blame her..."
Derek slowly lifted his head. His eyes were bloodshot, fixed on me, burning with rage.
"Chloe, I didn't think you'd sink this low."
I stood frozen. "I didn't push her. She fell on her own."
"You didn't push her?" He tightened his grip on the trembling woman in his arms and let out a bitter laugh. "Everyone in this room saw you grab her wrist."
"Camilla is too kind to even say a harsh word about you, and you still can't leave her alone."
"Is that what you do? Tear down anyone who's genuine, just to get my attention?"
There was no point in defending myself.
In his eyes, everything I did was wrong.
Derek looked down at me, his voice cold as ice.
"Since you refuse to change, you'll stay in the basement storage room until you've reflected on your behavior. You'll come out when you understand what you did wrong."
The butler hesitated. "Alpha, the Luna is terrified of the dark..."
Derek didn't even blink.
"I know."
"That's exactly why she'll remember this."
Chapter 3
"No!"
My eyes went wide with terror. I wanted to beg Derek, to plead with him.
But he just waved his hand impatiently. "Take her away."
The guards dragged me through the hall and threw me into the underground storage room.
The heavy iron door slammed shut behind me. The last sliver of light vanished.
Suddenly, I was drowning in pitch-black darkness. And with it came the memories.
In our second year of marriage, the rival Bloodmoon Pack had kidnapped me.
They locked me in a stone cell with no windows, no fire, no light at all. They demanded a ransom from the Thorn Pack, threatening to use my blood in some dark ritual.
I spent seven days in that suffocating darkness. No light. No sound. No way out.
I clawed my nails bloody. I screamed until my voice gave out. But no light ever came.
On the seventh day, Derek destroyed the Bloodmoon Pack. He broke through the cell door covered in blood, knelt in front of me, and spoke to me in a voice I'd never heard from him before, so gentle it broke my heart.
"Chloe, don't be afraid. I'm here to take you home."
After that, I developed severe nyctophobia. Even a sudden power outage would send me into convulsions, gasping for air.
Derek knew. He knew better than anyone. He'd been the one to pull me out of that darkness.
And now he was the one throwing me back in.
Back then, even a minute-long blackout would make him wrap me in his arms. He'd let his wolf warmth cover me and whisper, "Don't be afraid. I'm here. It won't be dark."
Now he'd locked me in the deepest darkness of my life.
I pounded on the iron door until my nails split and bled. No one came.
The darkness pressed in. I could feel hands reaching for me from all directions. I could hear screams and howls from the depths, monsters dragging me toward hell.
I screamed and sobbed, beating the door with all my strength.
"Derek, please let me out!"
"I didn't push Camilla! Please don't lock me in here... I'm begging you..."
Outside, the guards' footsteps didn't move.
"Luna, the Alpha gave his orders."
A cramp seized my lower stomach. I stopped moving, curled into the corner, and clutched my belly desperately.
Not long ago, I'd gone to the hospital for a checkup. The doctor had given me wonderful news.
"Ms. Chloe, congratulations. You're six weeks along. The baby looks perfectly healthy."
I'd folded the ultrasound into my bag. I hadn't told a soul.
I was waiting for the mate bond to end. Then I'd take this secret to a city where no one knew me and have this baby quietly, alone.
Derek didn't love me anymore. But this child was the Moon Goddess's final gift to me. The only thing in six years that was truly mine.
The darkness stretched on forever. My consciousness began to fray.
Before I passed out, I kept repeating to myself one thing:
Baby, I'm sorry.
Mommy will find a way to get us out of here.
Chapter 4
When I opened my eyes again, cold water hit my face.
The iron door was open. The light burned my eyes.
The butler stood at the entrance with two guards, his face grim.
"Luna, Miss Camilla has been poisoned. The Alpha requests your presence."
I could barely stand. The guards half-dragged me upstairs.
The master bedroom reeked of medicine. Camilla lay pale in bed, her lips tinged an unnatural blue. She was barely breathing.
Derek stood beside her, his eyes so red they looked like they'd bleed.
"Why did you do this to Camilla? You know wolfbane is lethal to werewolves. How could you poison her?"
"I didn't!" I said, my voice sharp.
He threw a bundle of wolfbane leaves at my feet. "The guards found this in your room. The evidence is right here. How much longer are you going to lie?"
The healer was urging him from the side. "Alpha, we can't wait any longer. Miss Camilla is in critical condition. The only option is to fight poison with poison, but the antidote might be harmful to werewolves. We need to test it on someone immediately."
Derek walked over to me slowly. He looked down at me, his voice cold and deliberate.
"Chloe, you're human. You're going to test the antidote."
"You hurt Camilla. You have to pay for it."
I was trembling all over. "Derek, please. I can't take that medicine—"
He didn't listen. He waved the guards forward.
They dragged me to the treatment room. I watched the healer walk toward me with the bowl.
I begged him. "Please, go tell the Alpha! Tell him I'm pregnant!"
"I'm barely two months along. It's his child! The antidote is harmful to werewolves—my baby has werewolf blood. I absolutely can't drink it!"
But the healer just sneered. "Luna, you're human. There's no way you could be carrying the Alpha's child. And even if you were, the Alpha wouldn't care. Miss Camilla is the one he cares about."
He gestured to the guards to hold me down.
The bitter liquid was poured down my throat.
At first, nothing happened.
A few minutes later, a sharp stabbing pain tore through my abdomen. Something hot and wet ran down my legs.
I collapsed on the floor, blood soaking through my clothes...
I woke up in a hospital room.
The doctor hesitated when he saw I was conscious. Finally, he lowered his eyes.
"Ms. Chloe, I'm so sorry. By the time you were brought in, the baby was already gone."
I lay there in silence. No tears. No screams.
I'd learned that when pain is absolute, there are no words for it.
Two days later, I was discharged.
I went through the D&C procedure alone. I handled all the paperwork alone.
When I returned to the villa, it was empty. Derek had sent everyone to the hospital to take care of Camilla.
I didn't pack any of my things. I didn't take a single valuable item.
I just placed the yellowed termination contract and the miscarriage report side by side on the nightstand in the master bedroom.
When I walked out through the front gate, the first light of dawn was breaking over the horizon.
I walked away from the cage that had held me for six years. I never looked back.
As the plane lifted off, I said my final goodbye to Derek in my heart.
Goodbye, my Alpha.
